news.title: Defeat against Iran and the illusion of American power
news.text:
America's military confrontation with Iran, more than anything else, revealed the limitations of Washington's military power; a reality that shows victory on the battlefield does not necessarily mean achieving political and strategic objectives. Now Trump has turned to economic pressure and blockade under conditions in which he has not been able to force Tehran to accept his demands.

In an analysis about American power and the consequences of the confrontation with Iran, Foreign Policy magazine writes: "The United States imagined itself as having a decisive superiority in military power as well as the ability to convert that power into sustainable political arrangements; while in reality, it possesses neither." This proposition can be considered one of the most important lessons of America's recent confrontation with Iran; a confrontation that once again revealed the gap between military power and the ability to impose political will.

Donald Trump entered the confrontation with Iran with the assumption that the military superiority of America and Israel could change the balance of power in a short period and force Tehran to accept Washington's demands. But the developments of the past months showed that possessing the most advanced military equipment, extensive destructive power, and the ability to carry out complex operations does not necessarily mean the possibility of achieving a desirable political result.

Failure in Realizing Strategic Objectives

 The main issue in assessing America's performance is not merely the extent of damages inflicted on Iran's military infrastructure; rather, one must ask to what extent Washington has achieved the objectives it declared for this confrontation.

At the start of the operations, the Trump administration had raised multiple objectives, including weakening Iran's missile capability, destroying its naval capacities, preventing Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon, and even providing the ground for changing the country's political structure.

However, the continuation of Iran's resistance and the persistence of fundamental differences between Tehran and Washington show that America's operational superiority has not been able to lead to Iran's political surrender.

The September 2026 report of the US Congressional Research Service also refers to this reality that the military confrontation has turned into a state of attrition and Washington still faces several difficult options, including continuing limited operations, intensifying military measures, or moving toward an agreement. In other words, despite possessing military superiority, America has still not been able to impose its desired political framework on Iran.

When Military Power Becomes a Strategic Cost

 Another important dimension of this confrontation is the costs America has incurred to continue it. According to the estimate of the US Congressional Budget Office, the cost of this country's military operations reached about 38 billion dollars by August 1, 2026. Pentagon oversight reports also indicate a reduction in munitions stockpiles and limitations in industrial capacity to replace consumed munitions.

This issue has strategic importance; because America's military power is not designed for only one region and one crisis. Washington simultaneously faces extensive security commitments in Europe, East Asia, and the Middle East. Therefore, the extensive consumption of weapons and the erosion of military capacities on one front can also affect this country's ability to manage potential crises in other regions.

On the other hand, the economic consequences of the confrontation have not remained limited to the region's borders. Disruption in maritime transit and the increase in concerns about energy security have transferred the costs of this confrontation to the global economy.

Under such circumstances, America has faced a strategic contradiction: to achieve its objectives, it needs to increase pressure, but the continuation of military and economic pressure also creates costs whose management becomes more difficult for Washington.

A Shift from Military Attack to Economic Blockade

 The developments of recent days are also an important sign of this situation. In its November 14 report, citing three informed sources, Reuters wrote that Trump has told his senior advisers that if Iran or Yemen's Ansarullah does not take provocative actions, he may for now refrain from new attacks against Iran.

This report also emphasizes that the American government intends to continue the naval blockade and economic sanctions while maintaining military options.

This change of approach must be analyzed within the framework of the difficulty of achieving Washington's initial objectives. Trump is now trying to force Tehran to change its calculations through economic pressure, restricting foreign trade, and creating increasing costs for Iran's economy.

But economic pressure also does not necessarily lead to the desired political result. The experience of international confrontations has shown that there is a difference between economic damage, change in political behavior, and strategic surrender. Exerting pressure on a country's economy is one matter, and forcing its political structure to accept the opposing side's demands is another.

The Great Lesson of the Confrontation with Iran

 What is important in the Iran file today is not merely the result of a period of military operations; rather, a deeper issue about the nature of American power has been raised.

Military power turns into strategic power when it can create specific, achievable, and sustainable political objectives. Otherwise, even great operational successes may lead to heavy costs and limited political achievements.

America still possesses extensive military power, and this reality cannot be ignored. Iran, too, faces economic pressures and damages caused by the confrontation. However, the criterion for measuring America's victory is not merely the extent of destruction of Iran's infrastructure; rather, it is the extent of Washington's success in realizing its declared objectives.

From this perspective, the recent confrontation has a clear message for American policymakers: one cannot break the political will of a country and impose one's desired order on it merely by relying on weapons superiority. America's strategic defeat is formed precisely in this same gap; the gap between the ability to strike and the ability to win.
news.summary: TEHRAN, Nov. 15 (MNA) –America's military confrontation with Iran, more than anything else, revealed the limitations of Washington's military power.

news.title: Trump Goon Hits Panic Button as Airport Chaos Spirals
news.text:
Sean Duffy is taking his show on the road—or, more accurately, to the Sunday morning talk show circuit.

President Donald Trump’s embattled transportation secretary, who has become the face of the worst aviation crisis since 9/11, is embarking on a four-network media blitz Sunday as the administration scrambles to contain the fallout from Friday’s nationwide ground stop.

Duffy, 55, is scheduled to appear on CBS’s Face the Nation, CNN’s State of the Union, NBC’s Meet the Press, and Fox News Sunday, giving him plenty of opportunities to attempt to reassure frustrated travelers that the administration has the situation under control.

But the former Real World star has already earned scathing reviews for his handling of the crisis, including from a longtime White House official who described one of his press conferences as “perhaps the worst” he had ever witnessed.

Richard Clarke, a former White House counterterrorism adviser who served under multiple presidents, told CNN on Saturday that Duffy’s joint appearance with Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin “did not inspire confidence.”

“It was perhaps the worst crisis communications press conference I have ever seen,” Clarke said, comparing it unfavorably with briefings by county sheriffs responding to active shooter situations.

Duffy has also faced calls to resign over his response to the four-hour shutdown, which has left airlines scrambling to recover and passengers facing days of disruptions.

And his demands for billions of dollars to overhaul the nation’s aging air traffic control system have drawn fresh scrutiny of his own voting record.

At a Friday press conference, Duffy demanded $50 billion in federal funding to modernize the system, despite having voted against a 2019 spending bill that included more than $10 billion for the Federal Aviation Administration during his time in Congress.

“The president’s asked for $30 billion. I want $50 billion,” Duffy said. “Let’s invest so we never have to come at 8:30 at night and have a press conference on why air travel was shut down.”

The secretary offered a possible explanation for the outage Saturday, suggesting a faulty wire switch may have been responsible, though the investigation remains ongoing. 

FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said investigators had found “zero evidence of anything nefarious,” pointing to an equipment failure rather than a cyberattack.

Meanwhile, Trump has remained out of public view since the crisis began, leaving Duffy to do the talking as the nation’s air travel system struggles to recover.

The Daily Beast has reached out to the Department of Transportation and the White House for comment.

news.title: Manila Hosts ASEAN Summit as Global Leaders Gather for Key Talks
news.text: Manila: Manila has become the centre of international diplomacy as regional leaders and prominent global figures gather in the Philippine capital for the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit.Discussions are expected to focus on major geopolitical, economic and security challenges affecting Southeast Asia and the wider international community.According to the Philippine News Agency, international delegations have been arriving ahead of the main event, with representatives from ASEAN member states, dialogue partners and international organisations scheduled to participate in high-level meetings from November 15 to 17.Among the early arrivals were Myanmar Foreign Minister Han Win Aung on November 12 and Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva on November 13.During his visit, Lula held bilateral talks with Philippine President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. The two leaders also witnessed the formalisation of agreements covering livestock, agriculture and the implementation of competition laws.The diplomatic arrivals gained momentum on Saturday with the arrival of Cambodian Deputy Prime Minister Hang Chuon Naron, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, Timor-Leste Prime Minister Kay Rala Xanana Gusmao, Vietnamese Prime Minister Le Minh Hung and Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese.According to the Philippine News Agency, Carney met Marcos to witness the endorsement of a joint framework committing the Philippines and Canada to a free trade agreement by 2027.Meanwhile, Albanese's visit is significant as Manila and Canberra seek to strengthen their bilateral defence cooperation.Other prominent arrivals included Lao PDR Prime Minister Saleumxay Kommasith, Brunei Sultan Hassanal Bolkiah, United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres, Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto, Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim, Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul and Singapore Prime Minister Lawrence Wong.The high-profile gathering has attracted leaders from beyond Southeast Asia, highlighting ASEAN's growing international diplomatic significance.Prime Minister Narendra Modi will also visit the Philippines from November 16 to 18 to participate in the ASEAN Summit in Manila, the Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) announced on Thursday.India is a strategic partner of the 11-member regional grouping, comprising Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand, Brunei, Vietnam, Laos, Myanmar, Cambodia and Timor-Leste.MEA spokesperson Rudrendra Tandon said that PM Modi would attend the 23rd ASEAN-India Summit and the 21st meeting of the ASEAN-led East Asia Summit process during his visit.He highlighted that India's engagement with ASEAN remains a key component of its Act East Policy, alongside its bilateral relations with all 11 member states.Tandon added that Modi's programme would include a dinner hosted by President Marcos for visiting dignitaries, participation in the ASEAN-India Summit and the East Asia Summit, as well as bilateral meetings with other world leaders.Alongside PM Modi, South Korean President Lee Jae Myung, New Zealand Prime Minister Christopher Luxon and Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi are expected to arrive on November 16.Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov and US President Donald Trump are scheduled to arrive on November 17. Trump is also expected to attend the ASEAN-United States Special Summit on the same day.President Marcos is additionally scheduled to participate in the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Summit, which China will host on November 18 and 19.The Philippine Department of Foreign Affairs has confirmed that Marcos will hold bilateral meetings with leaders from Australia, Brazil, Japan and South Korea. Consultations involving India, Laos and UN Secretary-General Guterres were still being finalised.The summit comes as the Philippines concludes its 2026 ASEAN chairship, a year marked by significant regional and international challenges.Philippine Foreign Affairs Secretary Ma. Theresa Lazaro described the country's chairmanship as a period shaped by multiple crises, including conflicts in the Middle East, natural disasters and growing uncertainties surrounding multilateral cooperation.Speaking at the opening proceedings of the ASEAN Foreign Ministers' Meeting on Saturday, Lazaro said the year had brought unprecedented challenges that tested the region's collective response.She emphasised that despite turbulent geopolitical conditions, ASEAN remained committed to navigating regional challenges and strengthening cooperation.President Marcos is scheduled to welcome visiting delegates on Sunday morning at the Philippine International Convention Center. He will deliver the inaugural address to formally open the summit plenary and Leaders' Meeting.

news.title: Global powers converge on Manila as ASEAN summit kicks off
news.text: MANILAA key regional summit opens on Sunday in Manila, with Southeast Asian heads of state facing questions on trade, security and an ongoing energy crisis while playing host to a who's who of global leaders.US President Donald Trump is scheduled to arrive on Tuesday near the summit's conclusion, a visit expected to include a sideline meeting with fellow Quad countries India, Japan and Australia -- the first of his second term.The meeting of the Quad -- a grouping broadly aimed at counterbalancing China's regional influence -- would come days before a historic sit-down with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russia's Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen.Brazil's recently re-elected Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, meanwhile, is set to attend a plenary session of the 11-member Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) on Sunday, while Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese will sign a new defence pact with host country the Philippines.Nearly 20,000 police officers have been deployed around Metro Manila for the summit, with progressive groups predicting a turnout of thousands on Tuesday for an anti-Trump march on the summit site.Much of the uproar targets the US Pax Silica programme -- a supply-chain initiative designed to counter China's dominance in semiconductors and rare earths -- whose flagship Philippine project, a 1,620-hectare AI manufacturing hub north of Manila, threatens to displace Indigenous families.US Ambassador to the Philippines Lee Lipton said last week that a widely rumoured November target date for a deal signing timed to Trump's visit was never in the works..PM Modi to travel to the Philippines next week for ASEAN and East Asia summits.Unfinished businessA day of early meetings kicked off on Saturday with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney announcing a Philippine trade deal, and ASEAN leaders huddling on key issues including haze from Indonesia and potential fuel-sharing schemes as members struggle with Iran war-driven shortages.But two issues that have vexed ASEAN leaders for years -- a languishing South China Sea "Code of Conduct" and their relationship with war-torn Myanmar -- look to be Singapore's problem when the bloc's rotating chair passes to the city-state in 2027.Myanmar has been excluded from high-level ASEAN meetings since a 2021 military coup that ousted the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi and triggered an ongoing civil war.Thailand, which shares a border with Myanmar and is leading the charge for closer relations, last week called for Naypyidaw's foreign minister to be allowed back into meetings.But Philippine foreign secretary Theresa Lazaro told reporters on Saturday there was "no easing" of the approach being taken with Myanmar, which faces an international ruling later this week on whether it committed genocide against its marginalised Muslim Rohingya minority.Hopes of achieving a so-called Code of Conduct in the disputed South China Sea between ASEAN states and China during Manila's year in the chair, meanwhile, have flagged.A Southeast Asian diplomat involved in summit preparations told AFP he did not expect a code to be signed at the summit.Lazaro indicated as much on Saturday, saying negotiations were "80 percent" complete."If it happens, then it's a small miracle," said Siew Mun Tang, former head of the ASEAN Studies Centre at Singapore's ISEAS-Yusof Ishak Institute..Hegseth proposes 'ambitious' US-ASEAN defence framework at Philippine summit.Shadow of BeijingBeijing claims most of the South China Sea despite an international ruling that its assertion has no legal basis, and its coast guard has clashed repeatedly with that of the Philippines.The row has reared its head at inopportune times over the past year, with a July foreign ministers summit opening less than a day after Chinese and Philippine sailors engaged in a clash.An ASEAN defence chiefs meeting last month saw Beijing send only an embassy defence attache, blaming "reckless" statements by Philippine politicians.A week later, Manila issued a rare rebuke to its own public officials over comments about China, stressing the need for a unified voice as the two countries negotiate.As the summit opens on Sunday, an annual seminar less than five kilometres (three miles) away will be making the case against China's South China Sea claims.Philippine defence chief Gilberto Teodoro, sanctioned by Beijing this year for what it called "irresponsible remarks", will give a keynote address..'Any code of conduct must comply with international maritime law': India amid news.title: US air travel should normalise on Sunday after ground stop triggers mass cancellations, FAA says
news.text:
Washington: Airlines canceled thousands of flights across the US on Saturday as they worked to recover from a nationwide ground stop that left passengers scrambling for seats and disrupted travel around the world.
The US air travel schedule should be back to normal by the end of Sunday, two days after what was the nation's longest ground stop in 25 years, Federal Aviation Administration Administrator Bryan Bedford said, declaring the "worst is behind us." The problem began when contractor L3Harris Technologies Inc. was replacing a section of the air traffic control system's old copper wire with new fiber wire, somehow causing the system to overload, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said.
The work led to "intermittent" communications and radar gaps, prompting the government to shut down air traffic for more than four hours. Officials were investigating whether contractor "incompetence" or a faulty router was the cause," he said.
"Our contractor didn't meet the moment or the equipment didn't meet the moment," Duffy said.
L3Harris said in a statement that it was supporting the FAA in the investigation to understand what led to the ground stop and the company takes seriously the impact to travellers, airlines and air traffic operations.
The FAA normally consults its own technicians in advance and asks them to assess the risks of any upgrades or repairs but that didn't happen in this case, the Professional Aviation Safety Specialists, the union representing the agency's technicians, said in a Saturday statement.
The nationwide stop was the first since January 2023, when a key FAA computer system that sends notices to pilots malfunctioned, and the second since the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks.
Andrew Charlton, an aviation consultant, said Friday's stoppage affected about a quarter of the 45,000 flights in the US each day.
"The knock-on effect of that is incredible," said Charlton, managing director of Aviation Advocacy. "The aircraft doesn't just fly from A to B and back â€¦ and then stop. It then moves onto C and then over to E and around and around and around. It is, of course, exacerbated if you're talking about long-haul flights, international flights over the Atlantic or over the Pacific."
Thousands of flights delayed and cancelled
At airports across the US, passengers scrambled Saturday to figure out how to reach their destinations. Some waited out the chaos in hotels while others sprinted to snag rental cars and bus or train tickets. Many camped out in airports.
Others got creative. Video in Seattle's airport showed a passenger serenading stressed out travelers with classical music. Stranded strangers in Lexington, Kentucky, participated in a cornhole tournament. The singer T-Pain and the band Hoobastank were captured on video singing to passengers as they waited on commercial airplanes.
Dan Russell, 66, learned his connecting flight from Hawaii to California was canceled a half-hour before boarding was scheduled in San Diego Friday night. Hotels were full, so he and his wife waited at the airport.
"There's nothing you can do," Russell said.
At the Newark, N.J., airport, Umi Egchi was trying to figure out when he could return home to Japan.
"I'm not sure exactly what happened. I just want to go home," said Egchi, who had a sleep mask on top of his head.
Sports teams that traveled for games this weekend adjusted game start times, and No. 19 Mississippi's football game at Oklahoma was delayed to Sunday.
FlightAware, a website that tracks flights, said more than 6,000 flights within, into or out of the US had been cancelled Saturday.
Officials say no one was in danger during ground stop
Duffy reiterated Saturday that no one was in danger as more than 3,000 flights in the air at the time of the grounding order landed safely.
Trump administration officials blamed Congress for failing to approve more money to replace decades-old technology that helps manage air traffic. Duffy said 70% of the system had been replaced, but his agency needs new air traffic control towers and runways.
The FAA has replaced thousands of old copper wires with fiber optic lines and upgraded hundreds of radio systems as part of the overhaul that began last year with USD 12.5 billion in funding. Duffy and the White House want USD 30 billion more to complete the work.
"We have aging infrastructure throughout the airspace," Duffy said, while stressing that flying remains safe.
Charlton, the aviation consultant, pointed to the difficulties of updating a system that can never shut down.
"What you're watching here is trying to change the tires of your car when the car's going at 80 miles an hour down the expressway, because nothing stops in aviation," he said.
Although Duffy said he had repeatedly spoken with President Donald Trump since the ground stop began, the president has not spoken publicly on the matter, nor issued statements via social media. He spoke on the phone with a Fox News reporter, but that was not on camera.
Past problems have been linked to equipment failures
The problem appeared similar to a regional air traffic control communication outage in September that snarled hundreds of flights across the Northeast. That disruption was linked to a construction crew cutting a fiber optic line.
Aging equipment was also blamed for brief radar outages last year that disrupted Newark airport.
Aviation safety expert Steve Arroyo said the difference Friday was the scale of the disruption that left controllers unable to reliably talk to pilots.
"If you don't have that ability, whether it's because the old wires that they have are just run down or for whatever reason, you've got to stop airplanes on the ground and not put them in the air," said Arroyo, a former United Airlines pilot.
news.summary: Thousands of flights were cancelled across the US following a nationwide air traffic ground stop caused by a communications network disruption. FAA officials expected operations to normalise by Sunday, while investigators examined equipment failure and contractor-related issues

news.title: Canada's Carney reports trade progress with Trump but says no deal yet
news.text:
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said Saturday that trade talks with the U.S. had advanced after a long call with President Donald Trump, but the countries had not reached a deal.

Speaking to reporters in Manila, the Philippines, Carney said Canada would not accept an agreement inconsistent with "a viable Canadian auto sector." The industry normally sends nearly 90% of its production to the United States, according to The Globe and Mail.

"There is a possibility of a deal, a bilateral deal, but we’re not yet there," Carney said.

Carney said earlier that, shortly before starting his current trip, he spoke with Trump and senior U.S. officials, including White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller and U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer. In Manila, he described the call as a "long, substantive conversation."

The Trump administration's view of the talks was not immediately known.

Auto industry in the negotiations

Carney said the Canadian auto industry's sustainability was non-negotiable and depended on continued access to the U.S. market. He described autos as both a fundamental issue in the negotiations and one of the most challenging.

"As I say, we’re making progress. We’re not there yet," he said.

Carney said the American industry also has an interest in the outcome, since its "longer-term competitiveness" depends on several factors, "including the degree of integration with the Canadian auto sector."

The Globe and Mail said Carney envisages a bilateral agreement that would reduce U.S. tariffs now applied to steel, aluminum and autos. The newspaper said he also reported progress on United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement, or USMCA, terms that would allow Canadian auto production to remain profitable.

A 25% U.S. tariff applies to Canadian-made autos, with an exception for U.S. parts in those vehicles.

Canadian passenger car and light truck exports to the U.S. dropped nearly 12% in value from 2024 to 2025, and are on course to fall further this year.

Canada left the negotiations in August after Carney said the Trump administration had made eleventh-hour demands Ottawa would not accept. The Globe said Washington had proposed cutting the headline auto tariff to 15% under a broader deal reducing Section 232 sectoral tariffs on several key Canadian industries in exchange for Canadian concessions.

Many Canadian auto industry figures rejected the proposal and welcomed Carney's departure from the talks, though the Globe said the decision left the sector with an unsustainable status quo.

The U.S. imposed 50% tariffs on $20 billion worth of Canadian exports after Canada walked away, The Hill reported. Canada retaliated, and Canadian officials pledged to match U.S. duties dollar for dollar.

"There’s lots of people who think that we should just go and take whatever deal," Carney said.

The government faces pressure to protect auto jobs as Stellantis seeks to sell its idled Brampton, Ontario, plant to an armored vehicle manufacturer.

On Friday, Industry Minister Mélanie Joly said Ottawa, the Ontario government and the plant workers' union had offered Stellantis an aggressive package and were "in solution mode to prevent the sale" to defense contractor Roshel Inc.

"The details of that and the implications of that will come out in due course," Carney said of the package.

Trade agreements in Asia

At the Manila news conference, Carney announced that Canada had substantially concluded free-trade negotiations with the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, or ASEAN, and completed separate talks with the Philippines. ASEAN is a bloc of nearly 700 million people.

Carney said the announcements were part of a strategy of "developing a dense web of reliable partners" and "reducing our relative reliance on the United States."

Canada is ahead of schedule on its goal of doubling non-U.S. exports in under 10 years, Carney said. He said almost one in three Canadian export dollars now comes from outside the U.S., a 40-year high.

Carney spoke before ASEAN's three-day summit in Manila, which Trump is scheduled to attend, The Hill reported.
news.summary: Carney said Canada would not accept a deal that undermines its auto sector, which faces a 25% U.S. tariff.

news.title: Federal judge blocks Trump's renovations of DC golf course hours before its closure
news.text: A federal judge issued a temporary restraining order Saturday to delay closing a D.C.-area golf course amid President Donald Trump's push to have the course renovated. U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes issued the two-week delay before the East Potomac Golf Links was due to close Sunday for 15 months. The course sits on federally owned land at East Potomac Park and has been part of Washington's public golf scene for more than a century. Trump announced in May the course would undergo a "historic renovation" that would prepare it to host major professional golf events. CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE The plaintiffs argue that Trump's plan would change the character of the accessible golf course and make it unaffordable, something the president denies. The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Trump has dubbed the course "Trash Island," doing so as recently on Saturday in a Truth Social post in which he said it is the "worst" course in the world. Trump said the conditions of the course are "very dangerous," adding pictures of what appears to be the course in poor shape. "The Fairways are far too close together. When you walk down the corridors of Trash Island, you don’t hear the sound of the running Potomac, all you hear is the sound of people screaming, 'FORE!'," Trump wrote. Trump has posted about the course in the past. Reyes in her ruling Saturday noted that Trump's posts presented a problem for the government. SIGN UP FOR THE DAILY OUTKICK NEWSLETTER "They indicate that the Washington National Plan is final and that [National Park Service] will close the Park to implement it," she wrote. "Both points favor granting Plaintiffs’ motion for another temporary restraining order." The park’s redevelopment is one of multiple projects in the nation's capital that Trump has championed to remake the city. They include a large memorial arch, a White House ballroom and the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts, among others. Reyes, who was nominated to the court by Joe Biden, had for months been reticent about approving the plaintiffs’ requests for work stoppages. The plaintiffs had argued the administration was moving ahead with work related to the project despite the pending lawsuit. Her reluctance to issue orders ended in October, spurred in part by a tree-cutting spree by the administration over a holiday weekend with little notification to the judge or plaintiffs. Officials and government lawyers said the tree work was part of a 2019 plan that recommended the cutting. In response, the judge confronted the administration over what she portrayed as deceitful actions over its intentions for the project. Reyes has repeatedly expressed frustration over the minute planning details she has been asked to adjudicate, including over the trees being cut down at the 106-year-old park. news.summary: A federal judge cited Donald Trump's Truth Social posts as key evidence when issuing a temporary restraining order on the East Potomac renovation.

news.title: Trump may avoid fresh Iran strikes if Tehran makes no new moves
news.text: WASHINGTON: US President Donald Trump is considering holding back from further military strikes on Iran if Tehran and the Iran-backed Houthi group in Yemen refrain from fresh provocations, according to people familiar with discussions inside the administration.Trump has discussed the possibility with national security advisers following intelligence briefings, but has not taken a final decision on how to proceed with the conflict that began with US and Israeli military action against Iran in February.Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan have also urged Trump not to resume attacks during recent conversations. The two leaders argued for restraint, but Trump did not commit to either course of action, according to people familiar with the calls.Washington has kept the military option open. news.title: US president may hold fire on Iran unless provoked
news.text:
Sympathetic to allies urging restraint; Saudi crown prince, Erdogan press Trump not to resume war• Mines hit three ships in Strait of Hormuz in two days; UN official urges Iran, US to let fertiliser shipments pass

WASHINGTON: President Donald Trump has told senior advisers in recent days that he may hold off on attacking Iran if the US faces no new provocations from Tehran or the Houthis in Yemen, according to three people familiar with the matter.

Trump has alternated between threatening new strikes and winding down hostilities since launching the conflict with Israel in February, and officials say he does not appear to have made up his mind about how to resolve it.

In meetings with national security advisers and after intelligence briefings, he said he was considering holding off on strikes and indicated sympathy for regional allies urging against full-fledged war, said the people, who spoke on condition of anonymity.

His private comments build on public remarks playing down the likelihood of major warfare resuming.

“I could end it immediately, but at the request of the nations that I am looking to protect, we are doing it a little bit longer way, a bit more civilly,” Trump told sports broadcaster Stephen A. Smith on Thursday.

Among those urging restraint are Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and Turkish President Tayyip Erdogan, who in phone calls over the past two weeks urged Trump not to resume attacks, arguing economic sanctions are working, officials familiar with the discussions said.

Trump told the Saudi crown prince on Oct 31 he planned to attack after the elections, but the crown prince pleaded for restraint.

US intelligence agencies have assessed that the naval blockade and sanctions are hurting Iran’s economy, while renewed strikes would not shift Tehran’s negotiating demands, two US officials said.

While Israeli officials continue to lobby for another military campaign, Trump signalled this week he may not need one.

Still, the Pentagon remains positioned to escalate. A third aircraft carrier is moving into the Middle East to replace one of two operating there, though all three could stay if needed, and Trump could opt to bomb Iran’s underground nuclear facilities again, though briefings warned precision munitions have drawn down.

A White House official said in a statement that Trump, as the sole decision-maker, holds all the leverage to protect US interests — backed by US control of the Strait of Hormuz and Iran’s collapsing economy. The official added that only the president knows what he will do next.

Even as Washington weighs its next move, volatile incidents continue in the Strait of Hormuz, where Tehran has restricted navigation since February and attacked noncompliant ships.

Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said on Saturday that explosions rang out on two oil tankers — including one supertanker — that had switched off their radar and positioning systems and struck a naval mine while attempting to transit the strait through an unauthorised route.

The report followed footage released on Friday showing smoke rising from a liquefied gas vessel the Guards said hit a mine in the south of the strait, bringing the tally to three vessels struck in two days.

The dual blockade of the strategic water way by US and Iran has disrupted global supply chains, prompting an urgent appeal from the United Nations on Saturday. Iran and the United States should “immediately” allow fertiliser shipments through the Strait of Hormuz to ease a crisis in vulnerable countries, Jorge Moreira da Silva, head of the UN Office for Project Services, told the COP31 climate talks in Antalya, Turkiye.

He called for an exceptional, time-bound solution allowing five fertiliser vessels daily.

Before the conflict, a third of the world’s fertilisers passed through the strait, and prices have since risen 30pc, he said. Missing planting seasons, he warned, could leave 45 million people facing acute food insecurity.

news.title: Pakistan, 16 other nations slam Israeli strike on Gaza hospital
news.text:
Condemn attacks on hospitals, tents sheltering displaced Palestinians• Joint statement says Israeli restrictions are worsening enclave’s humanitarian crisis

ISLAMABAD: Pakistan and 16 other countries on Saturday condemned an Israeli air strike on Nasser Hospital in southern Gaza, calling on Tel Aviv to protect civilians and medical facilities and ensure the sustained and unimpeded delivery of humanitarian aid to the Palestinian enclave.

The deadliest single strike since Israel’s elections last month hit the hospital’s surgery ward in Khan Yunis early on Thursday, killing at least six Palestinians, including a 13-year-old boy, and wounding nearly 30 others.

According to a joint statement issued by the Foreign Office, the foreign ministers of Pakistan, Algeria, Djibouti, Egypt, Indonesia, Jordan, Kuwait, Lebanon, Libya, Mauritania, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Somalia, Sudan, Turkiye and the United Arab Emirates condemned the Israeli strike in the “strongest terms”.

The statement said the strike “caused casualties among patients and medical personnel, in violation of international humanitarian law, which affords special protection to medical facilities and healthcare workers”.

It also condemned continued Isra-eli attacks on Palestinian civilians, including strikes on tents and other sites sheltering displaced people.

“These attacks undermine the ceasefire and efforts to restore security and stability in Gaza and are inconsistent with US President Donald Trump’s Comprehensive Plan,” the joint statement said.

Humanitarian aid

It expressed grave concern that “continued Israeli restrictions on humanitarian aid, shelter materials including tents, caravans and mobile homes, as well as medical supplies were deepening Gaza’s humanitarian catastrophe as winter approaches”.

“Inadequate shelter and deteriorating water, sanitation and healthcare services put civilian lives at grave risk, particularly those of children and infants, who could once again die from exposure to freezing temperatures,” it said.

The statement called on Israel to heed appeals from the international community and Trump’s Board of Peace for increased humanitarian assistance and to fulfil immediately and in full its obligations under the Sharm El-Sheikh Agreement.

“Israel must uphold the ceasefire, protect civilians and medical facilities, and ensure the safe, sustained and unimpeded delivery of humanitarian aid in sufficient quantities.

“It must also allow United Nations agencies and humanitarian organisations to carry out their mandates without obstruction.”

The ministers said the first-phase commitments were supposed to take effect upon the signing of the Sharm El-Sheikh Agreement.

“Israel must implement them without further delay or additional conditions, including political and security conditions, that impede humanitarian access,” the statement said.

“Urgent humanitarian assistance must proceed independently of progress on subsequent phases.”

The foreign ministers called on the US and the Board of Peace to “intensify their efforts to ensure Israel’s full implementation of these commitments and the lifting of all restrictions on the entry of humanitarian aid”.

news.title: Trump to broach nuclear cuts with Xi, Putin
news.text:
First three-way summit set for Thursday on Apec sidelines in Shenzhen• Iran war makes the agenda; Ukraine talks stay on a separate track• Musk to join US president on China trip

WASHINGTON: President Donald Trump will raise nuclear-arms reduction next week at the first three-way meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen, the White House said on Friday.

The leaders will meet on Thursday (Nov 19) on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit in the southern Chinese city.

“The president has made it clear that, among other topics, he will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world. This proliferation, President Trump believes, is very dangerous,” White House spokeswoman Olivia Wales told reporters on a call.

Trump’s insistence on focusing the first-of-its-kind talks on nuclear arms has riled Beijing, which is hosting a summit centred on trade and commerce.

China has resisted direct engagement with Washington on its nuclear programme, arguing it is more appropriate for the US and Russia to negotiate directly given their larger stockpiles.

The New Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty between Washington and Moscow expired this year.

A senior Trump administration official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said the US does not expect to reach an agreement in Shenzhen.

“This is a difficult topic for China to address, but we do think it’s time for China to sort of step up, you know, to the adults’ table, if you will, and have adult conversations about adult things,” the official said, calling it “the beginning of hopefully a conversation that can be productive going forward”.

Although nuclear weapons top the agenda, one major global conflict will also feature in the trilateral talks, while another will not, US officials said. Trump intends to discuss the US-Israeli war against Iran, but he is not expected to raise Russia’s war in Ukraine.

Washington has a “whole other track” of negotiations with Kyiv and Moscow aimed at ending the Ukraine conflict, the senior official said, noting recent talks between US envoys, Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky.

“China is not really a part of that track, so it doesn’t seem appropriate to have the Ukraine discussion there,” the official added.

Still, Zelensky has raised the alarm that the Shenzhen summit could echo the 1945 Yalta conference and result in a “redistribution of spheres of influence” for the 21st century.

Beyond the trilateral talks, Trump will hold a bilateral working lunch with Xi on Thursday, though he is not scheduled for a separate one-on-one with Putin or a meeting with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.

Officials also downplayed other potential flashpoints, with a second senior US official saying export controls on sensitive chip technology and former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation over an affair with an alleged Chinese spy are not expected to come up.

Meanwhile, Tesla and SpaceX boss Elon Musk will accompany Trump on the four-day Asia trip — starting Monday in the Philippines for an Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit — but will not attend the meeting with Xi and Putin.

news.title: US flight chaos caused by repair of old copper wiring: Trump admin
news.text:
Weary travellers endured more flight disruptions as service resumed at US airports after an hours-long total stoppage, with officials saying the situation should return to normal on Sunday.

The Trump administration blamed the mess that began Friday on a botched replacement of old copper wire communication lines.

The nationwide ground stop — meaning no planes can take off — sparked widespread chaos and left hundreds of thousands of passengers in limbo, with some pulled off planes moments before they were due to depart by airline staff who appeared in the dark about unfolding events.

“Tired. Exhausted. Frustrated. Yeah, you know, it’s just a mess, right?” Lisa Beraid, 48, who works for an insurance company, told AFP as she waited for a flight Saturday morning at New York’s La Guardia airport.

Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) chief Bryan Bedford said that 12,000 flights were cancelled on Friday and between four and five thousand flights out of 41,000 scheduled for Saturday were likely to be cancelled as well.

But as of Saturday evening, the tracking website FlightAware had recorded more than 6,200 cancelled flights.

Speaking at a news conference in Washington, Bedford offered a “sincere apology to the American travelling public.” He predicted a full resumption of flight schedules by “close of business on Sunday.”

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Friday’s four-hour ground stop was declared after maintenance work to upgrade an old copper wire to a high-speed fiber cable had caused “issues” with communication with airplanes and radar feeds.

“Either through contractor error or a faulty piece of equipment… it started flooding other routers in our air traffic control system,” Duffy told reporters.

In another embarrassment, Saturday’s news conference — where administration officials also appealed for more funds to upgrade outdated systems — was delayed due to technical problems with the audio feed.

Returning to normal

Friday’s disruption was only the second time such a ground stoppage had been issued in US airspace — which is among the busiest in the world — since the 9/11 attacks.

The nationwide halt was lifted at 8:15 pm Eastern Time Friday (6:15am PKT Saturday).

During the outage, footage from airports showed gates full, with planes waiting on taxiways and passengers thronging concourses, desperate for information.

FAA officials reopened the airspace “after restoring full functionality” at air traffic control facilities, according to Duffy.

Tim Johnson, consumer director at the UK Civil Aviation Authority, said although US flights have resumed, there could be “some follow-on disruption” as airlines re-book passengers and get all services back to normal.

At La Guardia airport, some travellers were more sanguine than others about the continued disruption of their flights.

“We’re stuck here for the next, I don’t know, 36 hours,” said Pat Curlett, a 62-year-old Ford worker.

“No one expects the whole airline system to go down,” said 77-year-old traveler Steven Rathe, who was waiting to embark on a four-leg trip from New York to Albuquerque.

“We’re lucky it wasn’t longer. So they’re flying today and for that I’m grateful.”

Ageing infrastructure

The ground stop not only plunged US air travel into chaos — it also raised serious concerns about the country’s ageing infrastructure.

Duffy appealed for $50 billion in funds to upgrade and modernise the air traffic control system, and called for Congress, which controls the purse strings of the US government, to “meet this moment.”

“Cut the crap,” retorted Illinois state governor and prominent Democrat, JB Pritzker, on X. “Trump and Republicans have controlled Congress and could have funded the system.”

New York Governor Kathy Hochul called on Duffy to resign or be fired by Trump, writing on X: “We’re fortunate no lives were lost.”

US lawmakers called for investigations into what caused the massive disruption and whether the country is adequately secure from cyber criminality.

“If today proves anything, it’s that we need to update our air traffic control system & rebuild our airport infrastructure,” Republican Senator Eric Schmitt said on X.

President Donald Trump was uncharacteristically quiet about the outage that had knock-on effects for international flights to and from the United States, making no public statement about the ground stop as of Saturday night.

news.title: Family Outraged After ICE Arrests Twin Brothers Described as Elite Athletes
news.text:
The parents of twin college soccer players described their shock after the brothers were arrested by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) while returning to their Alabama campus.

Wallace State Community College athletes Luis and Carlos Orta Santoro, both 19, were taken into ICE custody after a traffic stop on November 4 as they traveled back to campus, according to the Atlanta Journal-Constitution.

The Venezuelan twins had been visiting their parents, Carlos Enrique Orta and Reyna Santoro de Orta, in Georgia. They were arrested by a Lincoln Police Department officer during the traffic stop in east-central Alabama.

The brothers previously attended Archer High School in Lawrenceville, where they helped the varsity soccer team secure the school’s first-ever region championship.

‘This is the house of two elite soccer players,’ their father, Carlos Enrique Orta, told the outlet.

Luis and Carlos are seeking asylum after entering the United States legally on tourist visas, as their parents did.

Their visas later expired, but the twins were granted work permits and Georgia driver’s licenses, the outlet reported.

A Department of Homeland Security (DHS) spokesperson, whose agency oversees ICE, told Our News Outlet on Saturday that the brothers had entered the country legally on June 21, 2022, with temporary permission to remain. The spokesperson said they later ‘illegally overstayed in defiance of our laws.’

The DHS spokesperson told Our News Outlet: ‘All their claims will be heard by an immigration judge, and they will receive due process. This administration will not ignore the rule of law.’

‘To be clear, pending applications do NOT confer legal status,’ the statement added.

During their final year of high school, Carlos was named offensive player of the year, while Luis received the award for midfield player of the year.

The brothers began attending Wallace State this fall on soccer scholarships. They now face the possibility of deportation to Venezuela.

‘It’s been hell,’ their mother, Santoro de Orta, told the outlet.

She said she supported ICE removing ‘the criminals,’ but insisted that her sons did not belong in that category.

The twins’ asylum case remains unresolved, and they are still being held in custody.

Their mother said police told the family that the car had failed to make a complete stop at a stop sign.

The Lincoln Police Department entered into a partnership agreement with ICE in July.

According to the Cullman Tribune, ICE said the arrangement permits specially trained local officers to use limited immigration authority during routine police duties under federal supervision.

Luis and Carlos were booked into the Talladega County Jail on November 4 before being transferred to ICE custody the next day.

Their father, Orta, said the family had been struggling with feelings of guilt as they discussed what had happened to the brothers.

‘If anyone is at fault, it’s me. It’s us,’ Orta told the outlet. ‘Because I insist and I will continue to insist that Carlos and Luis came here because of a decision we made.’

He continued: ‘Carlos and Luis stayed here because of a decision from mom and dad. Carlos and Luis are here because of us.’

The Santoro twins were moved to the Pine Prairie ICE Processing Center in southern Louisiana after their arrest, WABE reported.

Nicolas Azcarate Florez, a friend of the twins, said he had spoken with them several times since their arrest.

‘They’ve been saying that they’ve been moved five times, so it has been difficult for them,’ Azcarate Florez told the outlet.

He described the brothers as players ‘that you could just give the ball to, and you would know that they would do something good with it.’

‘If we needed them, we would know that they would be there to help us out of a sticky situation,’ he added.

The arrests came during the same week that Republicans faced a historic blue wave in the midterm elections, widely viewed as a rejection of the GOP’s immigration policies.

After the elections, one of President Donald Trump’s first moves was appointing Stephen Miller as White House chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles.

Miller, one of Trump’s most loyal and longest-serving advisers dating back to his first administration, is known for his hard-line position on immigration.

Critics have described Miller as the architect of several of Trump’s most divisive policies, including the separation of migrant families during deportations in the president’s first term.

news.title: President Trump Scales Back Public Appearances as Iran Escalates
news.text:
The CIA has reportedly been warned by Mossad that Iran is planning to assassinate Donald Trump with explosive-laden drones.

The claim comes as the president has not made a public appearance since Wednesday, following a sustained series of rallies ahead of the midterm elections.

Israeli newspaper Israel Hayom reported that Mossad shared intelligence with the CIA indicating Iran may target Trump. The disclosure comes months after concerns over an assassination plot prompted the president to change planes.

Mossad chief Roman Gofman has held discussions with CIA Director John Ratcliffe in Washington this week.

Senior Israeli and US officials said the alleged plots have hindered peace negotiations between Washington and Tehran in recent days.

According to one senior official, Israeli intelligence believes the plan involves explosive drones.

In early November, Iran displayed a banner reading “We Will Kill Trump” above Enqelab Square in central Tehran.

Earlier this week, reports said Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent had become the latest cabinet official moved from his Washington, DC, residence amid Iranian threats against his life.

Attorney General Todd Blanche, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Secretary of State Marco Rubio have also been relocated to military housing.

Trump has not attended a public event for several days. He is expected to travel to the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China’s technology hub, for what would be an unprecedented gathering of leaders from the world’s largest nuclear powers.

During the summit, Trump is scheduled to hold trilateral meetings with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Our News Outlet has contacted the White House for comment on the reported plot against the president.

The White House said last night that Trump was receiving regular briefings about the FAA ground stop reported the previous night.

He has continued posting on his Truth Social account throughout Saturday.

Bessent was moved to a military base in recent weeks after intelligence officials determined that the threats against him had reached an advanced stage, The New York Times reported.

The seriousness of the threats against Bessent remains unclear, but they follow a broader pattern of Iran targeting US officials, including an alleged plan to kill Trump during the 2024 presidential campaign.

Bessent has led the administration’s economic campaign against Tehran as Trump confronts Iran.

The Treasury secretary has sought to isolate Iran by restricting trade routes and imposing tougher sanctions.

A Treasury Department spokesperson said Bessent “will not be deterred by the Iranian regime’s threats” and would continue pursuing the economic campaign against Tehran.

Bessent is among several Trump administration officials who have been moved from Washington housing during the president’s second term.

Bessent outlined what the “offensive” could involve in an op-ed for the Financial Times, directly warning countries that continue doing business with the Islamic Republic.

Calling the effort “Operation Economic Outcast,” Bessent said Trump had been “making phone calls to world leaders with specific requests to cease their interactions” with Iran and had already achieved results.

Trump’s promise to impose an “economic D-Day” on Tehran ultimately became a series of new warnings intended to cut Iran off from the global economy.

When asked why the US had not yet imposed secondary sanctions on Iran’s trading partners, Bessent said he wanted to give those countries time to move away from Tehran before it became too late.

Bessent has linked his own political future to the Iran conflict, privately persuading Trump to replace airstrikes with a sweeping sanctions campaign.

The conflict, however, has no clear endpoint, and the president told aides he expected another bombing campaign after the midterms.

At the same time, rising gas prices have kept inflation persistently elevated, while economic growth has stalled at roughly 2 percent.

A selloff in bonds has pushed the yield on 10-year Treasury notes to its highest point in more than two decades, despite a buyback program Bessent introduced to bring yields down. The benchmark yield reached 5.35 percent on Wednesday, its highest level since 2002.

The deficit has climbed above 6 percent of GDP—twice the 3 percent target Bessent presented to Trump—while the national debt has recently surpassed $40 trillion.

Trump, who reportedly speaks with Bessent almost every day, has continued to support him. At an event in Nevada, he once joked: “I created a monster.”

news.title: Judge Ana Reyes pauses Trump's 15-month East Potomac golf course closure
news.text:
U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes temporarily blocked the Trump administration on Saturday from closing Washington’s East Potomac Park and its historic public golf course, one day before the planned shutdown.

The order pauses President Donald Trump’s effort to turn East Potomac Golf Links into a championship venue, with the course previously scheduled to shut Sunday for 15 months. The administration cannot close the park or course but need not actively manage them, and the order runs through Nov. 28.

Reyes called the government’s reasons pretextual, writing that "the Government reverse-engineers additional justifications for the Park's closure… All while it continues to assert that it will close the Park to follow the President's directive."

It was unclear whether the administration would appeal or what would happen once the order expires.

Administration lawyers said the entire park needed to shut because the sea wall was deteriorating and the course posed safety risks. They also said nonprofit operator National Links Trust would cease running the course as of Nov. 15.

At Friday’s hearing, Reyes said safety had not entered the closure discussions for months and that ending the lease appeared to be a premise for shutting the park rather than a cause. Calling the absence of an operator self-inflicted, she said, "You're the one who set the house on fire."

Plaintiffs’ lawyer Catherine Carroll argued at the hearing that National Links Trust’s departure was no coincidence, given that Trump had directed the park to close the same day.

Reyes pointed to Marine Corps Marathon runners who went through the park in October. "If this is such an emergent situation… why wasn't [East Potomac] closed immediately?" she asked.

Justice Department lawyer Adam Gustafson argued that a closure would not bring immediate renovation because the National Park Service still had to conduct reviews for environmental and historic preservation.

Reyes said she plans to appoint former U.S. attorney for D.C. Jessie Liu to examine whether Interior Department and National Park Service officials and Justice Department attorneys breached ethics rules or misled the court. Gustafson asked her to reconsider.

"It's quite a cloud on the people it affects," Gustafson said.

"To be frank with you I don’t want to do this," Reyes said. "I think there is enough smoke that someone needs to consider whether there’s been fire."

The Justice Department opposes the appointment and sought Reyes’s removal, citing what it called her "egregious behavior." Reyes has not recused herself. Former President Joe Biden, a Democrat, nominated her.

Before the order, Trump wrote on social media Saturday that Reyes "doesn’t want us to quickly and inexpensively fix up the Course which is, also, very dangerous." He said Washington-area residents would receive a 50% discount at the rebuilt course.

Trump repeatedly called the course "Trash Island" in a Truth Social post and said the overhaul would attract tournaments including the U.S. Open and Ryder Cup, The Independent reported.

The DC Preservation League and two local golfers brought the lawsuit in February. They say the redesign would alter the accessible course’s character and make it unaffordable, which Trump denies.

"We are grateful that once again, a court has intervened to prevent irreparable harm caused by the Trump-Vance administration's pursuit of another one of the president's vanity projects," Carroll, of Democracy Forward, said after the ruling.

Trump announced in October that the course would shut Nov. 15 for a Tom Fazio design. The course opened in the 1920s and is about 2 miles from the White House. Fazio’s layout would run more than 8,000 yards from the back tees, The Hill reported.

The National Capital Planning Commission will consider the proposal at its Dec. 3 meeting.

news.title: Biden Reveals What Angela Merkel Really Thought of Donald Trump
news.text: Former President Joe Biden has shared Angela Merkel's private views of Donald Trump in his new memoir, revealing what the former German chancellor told him behind closed doors. In excerpts shared with Newsweek from Biden's forthcoming White House memoir, Promise Me, America, the former president recalls how Merkel candidly discussed her difficult relationship with Trump during their early conversations after he entered the White House in January 2021. The former German chancellor described Trump as "emotional," and questioned his fascination with Russian President Vladimir Putin and other authoritarian leaders, Biden writes in the memoir. Biden writes that Merkel was particularly frustrated by Trump's behavior during their meetings, including his refusal to shake her hand, and his apparent preference for personal impulses over established facts. "In our conversations... Angela was candid about her frustrations with my predecessor, who refused to shake her hand, and who seemed 'emotional' in their meetings, driven by mood swings rather than facts," Biden writes. "She also wondered why he was 'fascinated' by Vladimir Putin and other politicians 'with autocratic and dictatorial traits.' That was a mystery I could not unravel." The revelations offer a glimpse into the private conversations Biden held with one of Europe's most influential leaders as he sought to rebuild relations with traditional American allies following four years of Trump's "America First" foreign policy. Newsweek has reached out to Merkel and the White House for comment. Merkel's Difficult Relationship With Trump Merkel's relationship with Trump was frequently strained throughout his first presidency, with disagreements extending beyond their personal interactions to NATO, trade, climate policy and Germany's energy relationship with Russia. One of their most memorable encounters came during Merkel's first Oval Office visit in March 2017. Photographers captured an awkward moment when the two leaders sat alongside each other and were repeatedly encouraged to shake hands. Merkel turned toward Trump and quietly asked, "Do you want to have a handshake?" Trump did not respond, remaining seated with his hands clasped as cameras continued taking photographs. Merkel also reflected on the encounter in her 2024 memoir, Freedom, writing that she had initially approached Trump as though he were "someone completely normal." She described their interactions as feeling like "a competition: you or me." Their disagreements also became increasingly public. Trump repeatedly criticized Germany for failing to meet NATO's defense-spending target of 2 percent of gross domestic product, accusing Berlin of not contributing enough to the alliance and threatening to reconsider America's commitment to NATO. He also threatened tariffs on German automotive exports and criticized Germany's support for the Nord Stream 2 natural gas pipeline, arguing that Berlin was making itself too dependent on Russian energy. Merkel, meanwhile, opposed Trump's decisions to withdraw the United States from the 2015 Paris Climate Accord and the Iran nuclear deal. Following a contentious G7 summit in Sicily in 2017, she warned that Europe could no longer completely rely on others. "The times in which we could completely depend on others are, to a certain extent, over," Merkel said. Her comments reflected growing concern among European leaders about the reliability of the transatlantic relationship under Trump. Biden's Effort to Rebuild Relations With Europe Biden's conversations with Merkel formed part of a broader effort to restore confidence among American allies when he took office in January 2021. In Promise Me, America, he describes how he worked to reassure European leaders that Washington would once again engage with international institutions and traditional partners. Merkel, who had served as German chancellor since 2005, was approaching the end of her 16-year tenure. During Trump's presidency, she had increasingly become a central figure in European discussions about the future of the Western alliance. Biden writes that restoring those relationships was a priority, particularly as tensions with Russia continued to grow. His account of Merkel's concerns about Putin is particularly notable given the developments that followed. Biden reveals that U.S. intelligence agencies were tracking increasingly concerning Russian military movements around Ukraine throughout 2021, months before Putin launched his full-scale invasion in February 2022. He writes that he initially struggled to convince European allies, NATO members and Ukrainian officials that Putin was preparing to invade the entire country rather than pursue a more limited operation in the Donbas region. The president eventually shared intelligence about Russian plans for a coup in Kyiv, including preparations for a propaganda video that he describes as an elaborate, almost "Hollywood production" designed to manufacture a pretext for an invasion. Biden also recounts dispatching CIA Director Bill Burns to Moscow in November 2021 and personally confronting Putin in a phone call on December 7. Inside Promise Me, America Merkel is among several international figures who feature prominently in Biden's retrospective of his presidency. The memoir also contains candid accounts of his dealings with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, whom Biden initially questioned whether he had the experience and resilience to withstand a full-scale military crisis. Although Biden ultimately praised Zelensky's wartime leadership, he wrote they sometimes had a strained relationship, saying the Ukrainian leader could be "moody and stubborn" and "not as grateful as I would have expected" as he repeatedly pressed Washington for additional weapons and financial assistance. Biden also revisits the chaotic August 2021 withdrawal from Afghanistan in the book, writing that military and intelligence leaders had assured him the Afghan government and capital would remain standing for at least six months after American troops departed. Instead, that assessment collapsed within days as Taliban forces advanced and Afghan President Ashraf Ghani fled the country. The former president also reflects on meeting grieving families at Dover Air Force Base following the Abbey Gate bombing, which killed 13 American service members. He acknowledges that some relatives viewed him as responsible for their suffering and that several would never forgive him. Promise Me, America, published by Little, Brown and Company, is scheduled for release on Tuesday, November 17.
news.summary: Former President Joe Biden has shared Angela Merkel's private views of Donald Trump in his new memoir.

news.title: Judge Blocks Trump Administration From Closing Park in Golf Course Battle
news.text: A federal judge has blocked the Trump administration from closing a historic Washington, D.C., park and golf course, ruling that the government's stated reasons for shutting down the property were likely a pretext for advancing President Donald Trump's plans to redevelop the site. In a temporary restraining order issued Saturday, U.S. District Judge Ana C. Reyes barred the Department of the Interior (DOI) and National Park Service (NPS) from closing East Potomac Park and East Potomac Golf Course to the public, halting a planned shutdown that was due to take effect Sunday. The ruling marks another legal setback for Trump's efforts to transform the historic public golf course into a championship-style facility designed by renowned golf course architect Tom Fazio. Reyes found that the administration's explanations for the closure, including concerns about deteriorating infrastructure and the absence of a golf course operator, were likely pretextual, concluding that officials were seeking to close the park to facilitate Trump's proposed redevelopment. "The Court concludes that DOI and NPS plan to close the Park to further the Washington National Plan," Reyes wrote. The judge added that the government had acknowledged its intention to carry out Trump's directive to close the property, despite presenting other justifications in its formal closure announcement. During a November 13 court hearing, government counsel agreed when Reyes asked whether the administration was carrying out the president's directive. "You're carrying out the President's directive; right?" the judge asked. "Uh-huh, and that's the way the government works," government counsel responded. The dispute centers on Trump's plans to overhaul East Potomac Golf Course, a public facility situated on a peninsula between the Potomac River and Washington Channel. The proposed redesign, known as the Washington National Plan, would replace the existing course with a championship-style facility intended to accommodate major tournaments, including the U.S. Open and PGA Championship. Trump announced in October that restoration work would begin November 15, with the existing course closing to allow construction to proceed. But the administration's plans extended beyond the golf course itself. The proposed closure would have shut down large portions of East Potomac Park, including public roads, walking and cycling trails, fishing areas, picnic spaces, playgrounds and other recreational facilities. Reyes questioned why such a sweeping closure was necessary, particularly given that the government had previously allowed public access to the park despite longstanding concerns about the condition of its seawall. The administration cited the deteriorating seawall as one reason for closing the property. However, the judge noted that the National Park Service had identified safety concerns involving the seawall as far back as 2019 without previously determining that the entire park needed to close. She also pointed to the Marine Corps Marathon, which took place just days before the closure announcement and saw more than 30,000 runners permitted to travel around the park's perimeter. The court questioned why the government had allowed such a large event to proceed if the seawall presented an immediate threat requiring the closure of the entire area. "Maybe," Reyes wrote, referring to the government's argument that organized races in daylight posed different risks from individuals using the park during quieter hours. "But, even so, this does not explain why NPS now chooses to close almost the entire Park, at all hours, for an indefinite period." The judge also challenged the administration's argument that the closure was necessary because National Links Trust, the nonprofit currently operating the golf course, would no longer manage the facility after November 15. Reyes noted that the National Park Service had itself terminated the organization's continued operation of the course, then cited the resulting absence of an operator as justification for shutting down the park. "But that reverses cause and effect—by design," she wrote. The ruling found that the plaintiffs were likely to succeed on claims that the government had violated the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) and the Administrative Procedure Act (APA). In particular, Reyes concluded that the National Park Service had likely failed to follow its own regulations requiring notice-and-comment rulemaking before implementing a closure of such significant scope and duration. The judge also found that the administration had not adequately considered less restrictive alternatives, such as closing only areas immediately affected by seawall repairs or finding another operator for the golf course. "The Government proposes to close a historic park, daily enjoyed by Washingtonians of all stripes, indefinitely," Reyes wrote. "This closure would irreparably harm Plaintiffs, who use the Park regularly for recreational activities." Under Saturday's order, East Potomac Golf Course must remain accessible to the public, even if the government chooses not to operate it for golf. Other portions of the park, including Ohio Drive SW, must also remain open, with limited exceptions for immediate safety threats and areas where active seawall repairs require temporary restrictions. The order does not require the administration to operate the golf course or enter into a contract with a new concessioner. The temporary restraining order will remain in effect through November 28, unless the court issues another order. The ruling is the latest development in a legal battle over Trump's proposed changes to the historic property. The dispute has raised questions about the administration's authority to reshape public parkland, the environmental review process and the future of a recreational space used by Washington residents.
news.summary: A federal judge has blocked the Trump administration from closing a historic Washington, D.C., park and golf course.

news.title: Repair Of Old Copper Wiring Led To Hours-Long Flight Mess: Team Trump
news.text: Weary travelers endured more flight disruptions as service resumed at US airports after an hours-long total stoppage, with officials saying the situation should return to normal Sunday.The Trump administration blamed the mess that began Friday on a botched replacement of old copper wire communication lines.The nationwide ground stop -- meaning no planes can take off -- sparked widespread chaos and left hundreds of thousands of passengers in limbo, with some pulled off planes moments before they were due to depart by airline staff who appeared in the dark about unfolding events."Tired. Exhausted. Frustrated. Yeah, you know, it's just a mess, right?" Lisa Beraid, 48, who works for an insurance company, told AFP as she waited for a flight Saturday morning at New York's La Guardia airport.Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) chief Bryan Bedford said that 12,000 flights were cancelled on Friday and between four and five thousand flights out of 41,000 scheduled for Saturday were likely to be canceled as well.But as of Saturday evening, the tracking website FlightAware had recorded more than 6,200 canceled flights.Speaking at a news conference in Washington, Bedford offered a "sincere apology to the American traveling public."He predicted a full resumption of flight schedules by "close of business on Sunday."Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Friday's four-hour ground stop was declared after maintenance work to upgrade an old copper wire to a high-speed fiber cable had caused "issues" with communication with airplanes and radar feeds."Either through contractor error or a faulty piece of equipment...it started flooding other routers in our air traffic control system," Duffy told reporters.In another embarrassment, Saturday's news conference -- where administration officials also appealed for more funds to upgrade outdated systems -- was delayed due to technical problems with the audio feed.Also Read | Old System, Data Overload: What Led To US Grounding Over 8,000 FlightsReturning To NormalFriday's disruption was only the second time such a ground stoppage had been issued in US airspace -- which is among the busiest in the world -- since the 9/11 attacks.The nationwide halt was lifted at 8:15 pm Eastern Time Friday (0115 GMT Saturday).During the outage, footage from airports showed gates full, with planes waiting on taxiways and passengers thronging concourses, desperate for information.FAA officials reopened the airspace "after restoring full functionality" at air traffic control facilities, according to Duffy.Tim Johnson, consumer director at the UK Civil Aviation Authority, said although US flights have resumed, there could be "some follow-on disruption" as airlines re-book passengers and get all services back to normal.At La Guardia airport, some travelers were more sanguine than others about the continued disruption of their flights."We're stuck here for the next, I don't know, 36 hours," said Pat Curlett, a 62-year-old Ford worker."No one expects the whole airline system to go down," said 77-year-old traveler Steven Rathe, who was waiting to embark on a four-leg trip from New York to Albuquerque."We're lucky it wasn't longer. So they're flying today and for that I'm grateful."Aging InfrastructureThe ground stop not only plunged US air travel into chaos -- it also raised serious concerns about the country's aging infrastructure.Duffy appealed for $50 billion in funds to upgrade and modernize the air traffic control system, and called for Congress, which controls the purse strings of the US government, to "meet this moment." "Cut the crap," retorted Illinois state governor and prominent Democrat, JB Pritzker, on X. "Trump and Republicans have controlled Congress and could have funded the system."New York Governor Kathy Hochul called on Duffy to resign or be fired by Trump, writing on X: "We're fortunate no lives were lost."US lawmakers called for investigations into what caused the massive disruption and whether the country is adequately secure from cyber criminality."If today proves anything, it's that we need to update our air traffic control system & rebuild our airport infrastructure," Republican Senator Eric Schmitt said on X.President Donald Trump was uncharacteristically quiet about the outage that had knock-on effects for international flights to and from the United States, making no public statement about the ground stop as of Saturday night.(Except for the headline, this story has not been edited by NDTV staff and is published from a syndicated feed.)
news.summary: Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Friday's four-hour ground stop was declared after maintenance work to upgrade an old copper wire.
