news.title: North Korean leader's close aide visits Russia amid deepening bilateral ties
news.text: Digital Desk | Seoul, Nov 15 (IANS) A North Korean official considered to be one of North Korean leader Kim Jong-un's closest aides has arrived in Russia, the North's state media said on Sunday, amid deepening relations between the two countries following North Korea's deployment of troops to support Russia's war against Ukraine. Jo Yong-won, secretary of the Central Committee of the ruling Workers' Party, arrived in Moscow by private plane on Saturday, leading a party and government delegation, reports Yonhap, quoting the Korean Central News Agency. The visit comes at "a time when the militant friendship, friendship and relations of alliance between the Democratic People's Republic of Korea and the Russian Federation with independence and justice as their common ideal are being further cemented with each passing day," it said in an English dispatch. The delegation was invited by Dmitry Medvedev, chairman of Russia's ruling United Russia party. They were greeted at the airport by Andrei Klimov, a member of the party's Supreme Council and first vice chairman of the International Affairs Committee of the State Duma, the lower house of Russia's parliament, as well as North Korean Ambassador to Moscow Sin Hong-chol. Speculation that Kim could visit Moscow this year surfaced when North Korea's foreign minister made a surprise visit to Russia in July. Jo's trip comes days before US President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin are set to meet on the sidelines of an Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China, this week. Trump plans to discuss reducing nuclear weapons with the leaders of China and Russia during an Asia visit next week, but US officials do not expect the three-way meeting to produce an agreement. The meeting will conclude Trump's visit to China, White House Assistant Press Secretary Olivia Wales said during a briefing on his planned trip to the Philippines and China. A senior US official described the planned talks as the beginning of a conversation about reducing nuclear arsenals, rather than negotiations expected to yield an immediate pact. "We do not expect to get to any kind of agreement," the official said on condition of anonymity. Trump intends to discuss Iran during the meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, but Ukraine is not expected to be on the agenda, the official said.

news.title: New mechanisms required to prevent conflicts in Europe — US envoy Kushner
news.text:
WASHINGTON, November 15. /TASS/. The participation of the US allies in Europe in negotiations to resolve the ongoing Ukrainian conflict is necessary in order to create new conflict-prevention mechanisms within the NATO framework, US Special Presidential Envoy Jared Kushner said.

"NATO will remain a critical pillar of European security, enhanced by stronger mechanisms for military, communication, deconfliction, and reciprocal de-escalation, with practical ways to address disputes before they become crises," he stated on his X social network account.

"This is why we are working to bring our European partners directly into these discussions," the US official noted.

"Any final agreement must be agreed to by the relevant parties, and President (of the US Donald - TASS) Trump will only support arrangements that strengthen Ukraine’s and Europe’s security and make future conflict less likely," he continued.

Kushner added that "both sides understand that practical compromises will be necessary to end this war."

Russian Presidential Spokesman Dmitry Peskov stated earlier that negotiations with Europe would be required when the discussion turns to ensuring the security of Russia and Ukraine and the future of the security system in Europe.

Russia, the United States and Ukraine held talks in Abu Dhabi on November 10-11. Presidential Aide Vladimir Medinsky led the Russian delegation, while Foreign Intelligence Service chief Rustem Umerov headed the Ukrainian delegation.

US envoys Steve Witkoff and Kushner, NATO’s Supreme Allied Commander Europe Alexus Grynkewich and UAE Foreign Minister Sheikh Abdullah bin Zayed Al Nahyan were also present at the negotiating table when the talks began. Despite statements from French officials, no Europeans attended the meeting.

Kremlin Aide Yury Ushakov said European representatives consulted with the Ukrainian and US sides on the sidelines of the talks. He noted that discussions on whether Russia might meet with the Europeans and what form such a meeting might take would be based on the outcome of the Abu Dhabi talks.
news.summary: According to the official, NATO "will remain a critical pillar of European security," while these mechanisms are seen as a means of strengthening its capacities

news.title: Judo star Teddy Riner
news.text:
In a contest of who has the firmer handshake, it’s not a stretch to suggest, as he does, that French judo great Teddy Riner would get the better of Donald Trump if ever they were to meet as presidents of their respective countries.

But that’s a big “if.”

Even with five Olympic gold medals under his black belt and more than 3.3 million followers on his socials, Riner’s newly announced bid for the presidency of France is likely to be a harder contest than many of the judokas he crushed.

History and rules

stand in his way

The list of celebrities who successfully campaigned for elected office is shorter in France than in the United States, where Trump, Ronald Reagan, Arnold Schwarzenegger, Jesse Ventura, two-time NBA champion Bill Bradley, former Buffalo Bills quarterback Jack Kemp and others turned small-screen, big-screen and sporting stardom into political power.

Two-time Olympic champions David Douillet, in judo, and Jean-François Lamour, in fencing, and Guy Drut, the 110-meter hurdles champion at the Montreal Olympics in 1976, won seats in France’s parliament in retirement and served as sports ministers. But Riner is aiming to be the first celebrity to hold France’s top office since World War II hero Gen. Charles de Gaulle.

To appear on the ballot for the first round of voting in April, Riner needs a minimum of 500 elected officials to sponsor his candidacy, a requirement designed to not be easy.

The measure, intended to limit the size of the field and filter out fanciful candidacies, is an indication of how France has traditionally regarded running the country as a serious business. It has been in place since the 1981 election and was one of the barriers that foiled a presidential bid by comedian and actor Coluche that year.

“In France, there are complex hurdles to entry for people who don’t come from the establishment,” said François Hourmant, a professor of political science at Angers University who has studied celebrity culture in French and North American politics.

“Moving from the tatamis to the political arena isn’t that simple, and isn’t something everyone can do,” he said in a phone interview with The Associated Press.

Riner’s first

campaign stop

A thicket of cameras that greeted the 37-year-old on Friday, when he made his first campaign stop at a hospital in the northern suburbs of Paris, testified to the star power that Riner brings to the race.

Looking fighting fit in a dark suit and open-neck shirt, he towers over everyone from the height of his 2.04-metre (6-foot, 8-inch) frame. His imposing physicality and easy charisma translate readily to television.

But the policy proposals Riner plans to bring to the campaign remain unclear. He describes himself as neither left nor right on the political spectrum and says France “needs common sense” and not “a professional politician who recites lessons and squabbles all day long.”

In a two-minute, 37-second video that launched his campaign Monday and in an interview with the newspaper Le Parisien, Riner spoke of problems that he sees in France, among them “fear,” “anger,” a “social divide” and people unable “to envisage a future.” But he offered few solutions or blueprints for building what he called “the France that we want.”

Outside the hospital after meeting staff members, Riner said he is still working on his campaign platform and didn’t answer questions, responding with a “have a good rest of the day, au revoir” before heading back to his car.

Far-right candidate Marine Le Pen, widely seen for now as the favourite to succeed President Emmanuel Macron in May, took a gentle swipe during a campaign stop of her own on Friday, saying she couldn’t form an opinion about Riner’s bid without knowing anything about his platform.

As a dominant judoka whose mantra was “Never let anyone steal your beefsteak,” Riner told the AP in 2013 that he would sometimes wrestle up to five people at once in training to make it more challenging. As a fledgling politician, he says he is steeled for more rough-and-tumble.

“When you know how to take punches, you also know how to throw them,” he told Le Parisien.

An electorate hungry for

change but also experience

The rise of Le Pen and the challenge she faces from the other end of French politics from far-left leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon together suggest a swath of French voters want deep and disruptive change.

But analysts believe many also want a seasoned hand to deal with the multitude of domestic and international challenges that France faces, including its record public debt and the threat to European security posed by Russian President Vladimir Putin and his war in Ukraine.

“Teddy Riner certainly embodies renewal, but he doesn’t necessarily embody experience. So that is probably one of his main disadvantages,” said Mathieu Gallard, research director at the Ipsos polling institute.

Riner, who is black, was born on the French Caribbean island of Guadeloupe and grew up in Paris. Both Gallard and Hourmant said the potential that Riner is more likely to understand and combat discrimination could attract people of colour in an election where Le Pen’s party and others on the far right are again seeking to focus on immigration.

“But again, is that enough to translate into votes,” Gallard asked.

“Teddy Riner’s skin colour will be a political issue for some people,” Hourmant said. For some, “it may be a reason to support him, seeing a racialised candidate from the overseas territories. For others, it will be a deterrent.”

news.title: Carney awarded ‘Democracy Medal’ by global group of political strategists
news.text:
The International Association of Political Consultants is set to give its 2026 Democracy Medal to Prime Minister Mark Carney, Global News has learned.

Carney, travelling in Asia for the next several days, was unable to accept the award in person, which was to be announced Saturday evening at the International Association of Political Consultants’ (IAPC) annual conference in Seville, Spain.

Previous winners of the IAPC’s Democracy Medal include Russian democracy activist Alexei Navalny, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, and South Africa’s Nelson Mandela.

The IAPC was established in 1968 and it first presented a Democracy Medal in 1982 to Polish Solidarity leader Lech Walesa. The IAPC has about 180 members worldwide who work as political consultants, strategists and pollsters.

“The IAPC Democracy Medal 2026 goes to Prime Minister Mark Carney because, at a time when the political landscape is shifting faster than at any point in a generation, he offered the world something rare: clarity,” IAPC President Marko Rakar said in a draft statement reviewed by Global News.

“He did not raise his voice; he raised the standard. With calm and clear thinking, he showed that middle powers are not powerless, and that working together they can defend the rule of law, honour the obligations nations owe one another, and help keep the international order and the peace it protects.”

Carney’s hallmark foreign policy speech so far in his 18-month tenure as prime minister was given at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, on Jan. 20. In the speech, Carney argued that middle powers, like Canada, should reject the power of ‘hegemons’ and build coalitions with like-minded partners.

Carney did not mention either the United States or China by name as the ‘hegemons’ that had caused a “rupture” in the international order.

But he issued a call to action at Davos to middle powers in Europe and Asia: “In a world of great power rivalry, the countries in between have a choice: to compete with each other for favour or to combine to create a third path with impact,” Carney said. “We should not allow the rise of hard power to blind us to the fact that the power of legitimacy, integrity, and rules will remain strong — if we choose to wield it together.”

Carney has built on some of the themes of his Davos speech in subsequent speeches in international fora, including, for example, at the European Parliament in Strasbourg, France earlier this fall.

“Our members nominated him and our membership chose him, because democracy needs leaders who tell the truth about the world as it is and still work for the world as it should be,” the IAPC’s Rakar said in the draft release.

Carney, who started the day Sunday at the ASEAN Summit in Manila, The Philippines and will end the day at the Francophonie Summit in Phnom Penh, Cambodia, did not immediately respond to comment about the IAPC’s award.

After Cambodia, Carney travels to Shenzhen, China, for the annual summit of Pacific nation leaders known as APEC to be hosted by Chinese President Xi Jinping. U.S. President Donald Trump is also expected to attend.
Carney says he expects to have a one-on-one meeting with Xi but it is unclear if he will meet separately with Trump.
news.summary: A group of global political consultants and strategists say Prime Minister Mark Carney's "clarity" and "calm and clear thinking" was worthy of international recognition.

news.title: Hall of Fame quarterback Fran Tarkenton splashes out on $52million mansion in ritzy billionaire Florida neighborhood
news.text:
Pro Football Hall of Famer Fran Tarkenton forked out a staggering fee for a luxury mansion in an exclusive oceanfront neighborhood in Florida, according to reports. 

Tarkenton, 86, is said to have splashed out $51.9 million on the opulent estate, buying the Mediterranean-style property from garbage-and-recycling mogul Anthony Lomangino this week, according to The Palm Beach Post. 

The two-story home sits on the ritzy stretch of road on Ocean Boulevard known as Billionaires Row in the affluent South Florida town. 

Situated on the seafront, the home boasts breathtaking views of the pristine ocean as well as private beach access. 

The beautiful home, built in 2006, features five bedrooms and eight bathrooms across 8,723 square feet of living space. 

The primary suite features sitting room, wet bar, dual baths and closets, and oversized east-facing balcony providing commanding water views. 

A sophisticated formal living room offers similar unrivaled views, while the layout also includes a paneled library, dining room and chef's kitchen equipped with a gorgeous La Cornue stove, oversized island with seating for ten, and breakfast room. 

The more than half an acre of land boasts a newly built courtyard pool and spa, and three-car garage, while French doors open onto a romantic covered loggia with fireplace and marble columns. 

The lavish mansion also sits around a mile away from Donald Trump's Mar-a-Lago resort. Tarkenton was a supporter of the President during his 2016 campaign. 

Other features of the house include a card room, an elevator and a three-car garage. 

Tarkenton played quarterback in the NFL for 18 seasons, suiting up for both the Minnesota Vikings and the New York Giants. 

He is best remembered for leading the Vikings to three Super Bowl appearances and winning the NFL MVP award in 1975. 

He retired from the NFL in 1979, finishing his career as the league's all-time leader in passing yards and touchdowns. He was inducted into the Pro Football Hall of Fame in 1986. 

After hanging up his cleats, Tarkenton went on to pursue a number of business ventures. He also provided commentary for 'Monday Night Football' from 1979 to 1982.

Lomangino bought the property in 2019 for $12.65 million before undertaking extensive renovations on the home. 

He and his family reportedly bought an iconic seaside home up the road for $76.74 million earlier this year.

news.title: Haiti welcomes troops from El Salvador’s hard-line president as gang violence rages
news.text: In March 2024, when armed gangs in Haiti joined forces and parts of the battered country’s capital went up in flames, El Salvador’s President Nayib Bukele wrote on X: “We can fix it.” Bukele, who waged war on gangs in El Salvador without legal constraints and built what is considered one of the world’s largest and most brutal prisons, was not joking. Two and a half years later, following the abduction of four Salvadoran soldiers serving in Haiti as part of an international U.N. force, Bukele is making his move. In the poorest country in the Western Hemisphere, desperate residents are grateful for any help, even if it comes from a brutal dictator. Bukele, 45, was born in San Salvador to a father of Palestinian Christian descent whose family originated in Bethlehem and a mother of Spanish descent. After receiving direct approval in a phone call with U.S. President Donald Trump, Bukele sent more than 2,000 troops to Haiti last week. On Thursday, he posted a video on X showing soldiers and military equipment boarding aircraft, writing: “This is not an operation against the Haitian people, nor an invasion of the country of Haiti. We went through the same suffering that Haiti is going through today. But we managed to escape it.” The military operation, which is being conducted outside the framework of the U.N.-backed mission, is a highly unusual move and a major gamble for Bukele. If it succeeds, he will become the man who rescued the Caribbean nation from an an endless cycle of violence and bloodshed. More than 5,000 murders have been recorded there this year, while other countries have refused to offer assistance. The price, however, is likely to be steep, as Bukele has shown little concern for the safety of innocent civilians. His strategy for eliminating gangs in El Salvador included mass incarceration at the prison known as CECOT, where tens of thousands of inmates were sent, many without due process. The Trump administration used the notorious prison to hold migrants deported from the United States, including people with no criminal records and others who had been in the U.S. legally. About a decade ago, El Salvador’s murder rate was appallingly high. International troops arrived in Haiti in April, but the force currently numbers only about 2,000 personnel, far short of the 5,500 promised. The four Salvadoran soldiers came under fire and were abducted while traveling through a gang stronghold in Haiti. They have not been seen since. Bukele initially dispatched several hundred special forces troops to assist in the search, but since October 22, he has deployed an additional 2,500 troops, including special forces personnel. The fate of the missing soldiers remains unknown. Haiti’s violent gang leaders did not take the development quietly. Last week, Wilson Joseph, leader of the 400 Mawozo gang and a suspect in the abduction of the Salvadoran soldiers, declared that he was ready to fight and would be "waiting for you”, referring to Bukele. Naturally, Bukele, who is highly adept at using social media, could not ignore the challenge. After photographs of Joseph’s lavish mansion began circulating online, Bukele asked his followers in Haiti: “Where is this house? Give us the exact address and we’ll destroy it.” Two days later, the house was attacked. Video footage showed men fleeing the building, which was partially engulfed in flames. About 20 people were killed, but Joseph himself appears to have escaped. Amnesty International issued a statement shortly after the attack, saying: “The Prime Minister of Haiti, Alix Didier Fils-Aimé, and the President of El Salvador, Nayib Bukele, must ensure that all operations conducted by Salvadoran forces in Haiti comply with international human rights law.” But Bukele remains unfazed. For years, he has dismissed human rights organizations, calling them “law firms for criminals.” He also enjoys considerable support in Haiti. Crowds turned out to welcome the forces he dispatched, and for hours, chants of “Bukele” rang through the exhausted streets of the capital, Port-au-Prince. One local resident told The New York Times that Haitians were desperate for relief and increasingly looked to outside forces for salvation.
news.summary: El Salvador’s President Nayib Bukele has sent thousands of troops to gang-ravaged Haiti, drawing cheers from desperate residents; His brutal crackdown on crime at home raises fears of civilian casualties as he seeks to restore order

news.title: Judge temporarily blocks Trump from moving ahead on Washington public golf course redevelopment
news.text:
A federal judge on Saturday ordered a temporary stop to any work at a historic Washington public golf course not far from the White House, blocking for now President Donald Trump's push to redevelop the site along the Potomac River into a championship-level venue.

U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes issued the temporary restraining order before the East Potomac Golf Links was due to close Sunday for 15 months. Trump had announced work would begin that day despite the legal challenge initiated against the project in February by the DC Preservation League and two local golfers.

The plaintiffs argue that Trump's plan would change the character of the accessible golf course and make it unaffordable, something the Republican president denies. They had sought the stop-work order, saying that closing the course and launching work on the project would “irreparably injure plaintiffs and the public interest."

The park’s redevelopment is one of multiple projects in the nation's capital that Trump has championed to remake the city. They include a large memorial arch, a White House ballroom and the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts, among others. 

Reyes had signaled throughout a five-hour court hearing Friday that she was likely to issue some stoppage for the park closure. The only issue was how expansive it might be. Justice Department lawyer Adam Gustafson argued that the entire East Potomac Park, which includes three golf courses, a miniature course, bike riding lanes and other recreational areas, was being closed because of safety factors. He also noted that the lease between the government and the current operator, National Links Trust, was ending Sunday.

Reyes pointed out that safety had not been part of the discussion over the closure for months and that ending the lease felt more like an action that provided a premise for the closure rather than an action that led to the closure of the course about 2 miles from the White House.

She also rejected Gustafson's argument that the closure was separate from Trump's repeated pronouncements that he wanted the course to be closed and renovated into a world-class venue and had called repeatedly for the park's closure by the deadline as part of what is known as the Washington National plan.

Even before the order, Trump lashed out in a social media post Saturday, contending that Reyes “doesn’t want us to quickly and inexpensively fix up the Course which is, also, very dangerous.” He said people who live in the Washington area would get a 50% discount on “any and all Rates charged” and that the redevelopment would “evolve into something very special, something which the Judge will be able to take great pride in seeing!”

Reyes’ order was the latest in a series of rulings in lawsuits challenging Trump’s projects that were issued just hours before construction was expected to begin. A different judge recently ordered a 14-day delay on work for the arch, a decision that came shortly after a key planning commission stacked with Trump appointees approved plans for the project. 

Reyes, who was nominated to the court by Democratic President Joe Biden, had for months been reticent about approving the plaintiffs’ requests for work stoppages. The plaintiffs had argued the administration was moving ahead with work related to the project despite the pending lawsuit.

Her reluctance to issue orders ended in October, spurred in part by a tree-cutting spree by the administration over a holiday weekend with little notification to the judge or plaintiffs. 

Officials and government lawyers said the tree work was part of a 2019 plan that recommended the cutting. In response, the judge confronted the administration over what she portrayed as deceitful actions over its intentions for the project.

Reyes has repeatedly expressed frustration over the minute planning details she has been asked to adjudicate, including over the trees being cut down at the 106-year-old park. The Justice Department filed a request that Reyes be removed from the case because of what it called her “egregious behavior” and questioned her impartiality. Reyes has not recused herself. 

The restraining order was one of two issues Reyes took up during Friday's hearing.

She announced plans last week to name Jessie Liu, a former U.S. attorney for the District of Columbia, to examine whether officials with the Interior Department and the National Park Service and attorneys with the Justice Department had violated ethics or misled her during the course of the case. Gustafson asked her to reconsider and give the Justice Department the opportunity to show an outside investigator was unnecessary. 

“It's quite a cloud on the people it affects,” he said. 

Reyes said she understood. 

“To be frank with you I don’t want to do this,” she said, but she had an ethical obligation to at least look because "I think there is enough smoke that someone needs to consider whether there’s been fire.”
news.summary: A federal judge has ordered a temporary stop to any work at a historic Washington public golf course not far from the White House

news.title: Family's fury as 'elite' athlete twin brothers are arrested by ICE while on their way to college in Alabama
news.text:
A dismayed mother and father spoke out after their 'elite' athlete twin sons were arrested by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) as they returned to their Alabama college.

Wallace State Community College soccer players Luis and Carlos Orta Santoro, 19, were taken into ICE custody after a traffic stop on November 4 while on their way to campus, the Atlanta Journal-Constitution reported.

The Venezuelan twins were returning from visiting their parents, Carlos Enrique Orta and Reyna Santoro de Orta, in Georgia when they were arrested by a Lincoln Police Department officer during a traffic stop in east-central Alabama.

The brothers graduated from Lawrenceville's Archer High School after a successful varsity soccer career that included a first ever region title for the school.

'This is the house of two elite soccer players,' Carlos Enrique Orta, their father, told the outlet.

Luis and Carlos are asylum seekers who applied for protections after legally entering the US on a tourist visa, like their parents.

That visa expired and the twins were granted US work permits and Georgia driver's licenses, according to the outlet.

A spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which oversees ICE, told the Daily Mail on Saturday that the brothers had legally entered the US with permission to stay on a temporary basis on June 21, 2022, but then 'illegally overstayed in defiance of our laws.'

The DHS spokesperson told the Daily Mail: 'All their claims will be heard by an immigration judge, and they will receive due process. This administration will not ignore the rule of law.'

'To be clear, pending applications do NOT confer legal status,' the statement continued.

Carlos was named the offensive player of the year and Luis the midfield player of the year by their high school this year.

They had received soccer scholarships to attend Wallace State, which they began doing this fall, but now face deportation to Venezuela.

'It's been hell,' Santoro de Orta, their mother, told the outlet.

She added that she supported ICE 'taking away the criminals' but said her children did not fit that description.

A final decision on the brothers' asylum case is still pending as they remain in custody.

The concerned mother claimed police said the twins' car had failed to come to a complete stop at a stop sign.

The Lincoln Police Department signed a partnership agreement with ICE in July.

ICE said the program allows trained local officers to exercise limited immigration authority during routine police work under federal supervision, according to the Cullman Tribune.

Luis and Carlos were booked into the Talladega County Jail on November 4 and transferred to ICE custody the following day.

Their father, Orta, described how the family was grappling with guilt as they shared what happened to their children.

'If anyone is at fault, it's me. It's us,' Orta told the outlet. 'Because I insist and I will continue to insist that Carlos and Luis came here because of a decision we made.'

He added: 'Carlos and Luis stayed here because of a decision from mom and dad. Carlos and Luis are here because of us.'

The Santoro twins were taken to the Pine Prairie ICE Processing Center in southern Louisiana after their arrest, WABE reported.

A friend of the twins, Nicolas Azcarate Florez, said he had spoken to them multiple times since they were taken into custody.

'They've been saying that they've been moved five times, so it has been difficult for them,' Azcarate Florez told the outlet.

Azcarate Florez said the brothers were 'players that you could just give the ball to, and you would know that they would do something good with it.'

'If we needed them, we would know that they would be there to help us out of a sticky situation,' he added.

The brothers were taken into custody on the same week that the Republican Party faced a historic blue wave in the midterm elections that was seen as a rebuke of the GOP's immigration policy.

One of President Donald Trump's first moves afterwards was to name Stephen Miller as the new White House chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles.

Miller, one of Trump's most loyal and longest-serving advisers going back to his first administration, is known for his hardline views on immigration.

Critics have cited Miller as the architect of some of Trump's most divisive policies, including separating migrant families during deportations in the President's first term.
news.summary: The Venezuelan twins were returning from visiting their parents in Georgia when they were arrested by a Lincoln Police Department officer during a traffic stop.

news.title: Hundreds of men march in Switzerland to protest violence against women  - Guyana Inquirer – Daily Guyana News
news.text:
Hundreds of men have led a demonstration in Switzerland’s capital, Bern, to denounce misogyny and violence against women, saying men need to take a more effective role in fighting both.

The “Men Against Violence Against Women” rally outside parliament on Saturday follows persistent concerns that misogyny is too prevalent online among teenage boys and young men and that other men need to build a stronger counter-narrative.

The misogynistic views are pushed by the right-wing “manosphere” – a loose network of online forums and influencers that promote male supremacy and hostility to feminism. Such influencers were emboldened after Donald Trump won the US presidential election in 202 to justify and amplify misogynistic derision and threats online.

“We men are part of the problem – the problem being violence against women and queer people,” said Christoph Gosteli, a 42-year-old social worker who co-organised the rally with a group called maenner.

“That is why it is important for us to take a stand and say, ‘We no longer want to be part of the problem; we want to be part of the solution.’”

An academic and advocacy group survey released in June by the University of Zurich and MenCare, an umbrella group of Swiss men’s and fathers’ organisations, found that half of male respondents aged 18 to 24 held a “restrictive and dominance-based view of masculinity”, expressing concerns that “real men are increasingly marginalised in society”.

The study called for “a systematic and society-wide debate about ideals of masculinity that promote violence”, beginning in schools.

Swiss Justice Minister Beat Jans attended a conference earlier this month on the dangers of violent online abuse of women.

In a speech on November 2, he said that men commit four-fifths of violent crimes and that in rape cases, the share is “as high as 99 percent”.

“It is not all men. But we must also admit: It is almost always men,” Jans said. “Violence by men does not begin with the first blow; it begins with a disparaging remark. We men all have a duty.”

news.title: Midterms, gas prices and the nuclear threat from Iran
news.text:
The impact of the Iran conflict on the midterm elections reveals a deep malaise in the American psyche that makes us vulnerable to our enemies. If an extra dollar per gallon and 1% higher inflation for a year or so is too heavy a burden to end a nuclear threat, the old Soviet saying that “when it comes time to hang the capitalists, they will sell us the rope” sounds about right.

In June 2025, Israel’s war with Iran ended when the U.S. bombed three Iranian nuclear facilities in Operation Midnight Hammer. After Iran’s continued aggression, and reports that it massacred up to 30,000 of its own citizens and restarted its nuclear program, on Feb. 28, Donald Trump launched Operation Epic Fury. Its goals were to ensure that Iran could never acquire nuclear weapons; to destroy its missile capabilities and navy; to prevent it from arming, funding and directing terrorist proxies; and to offer hope to the Iranian people.

Epic Fury made considerable progress, but after 38 days Trump declared a ceasefire. Since then, the U.S. has blockaded Iranian ports, imposed economic sanctions, and sporadically attacked Iranian military installations and skirmished with Iranian forces.

In assessing the Iran conflict, Americans have splintered into several camps:

Islamists, communists, progressives, antisemites, and conspiracy theorists argue that Iran was not close to obtaining a nuclear weapon before the U.S. attack on Feb. 28 and had promised not to pursue one. Many of these critics insist that Iran has the same right as any other country to develop nuclear weapons and the world “needs” an Iranian nuclear bomb to balance Israel.
Traditional liberals, moderates, and some Republicans argue that although Iran should not obtain a nuclear weapon, the process leading up to the Feb. 28 attack was flawed. At least some of these critics might have supported an attack that had buy-in from Congress and foreign allies, preferably after the midterm elections. They believe the price increases caused by the conflict were a major factor in the Republicans’ election drubbing. The day after the midterms, JD Vance, who opposed the mission, posted on X that the Iran War and Israel are at fault for Republicans’ midterm losses.

Both of these groups also point to Trump’s boast that that Midnight Hammer “obliterated” Iran’s nuclear capability.

Those who supported the Feb. 28 attack argue that the United States should have stayed the course. Though many in this camp question whether the logistics and supply operations were up to the task and whether the timeline for completion was realistic, and some endorse the transition to a blockade and sanctions, most supporters believe that had Trump resumed combat operations, the United States would already have downsized its deployments in the Middle East, the Strait of Hormuz would be open, and oil, gas, and agriculture prices would be on the way to pre-war levels. They believe that the conflict has become a low-intensity quagmire that is allowing Iran to rebuild its capabilities.

To most supporters of Midnight Hammer and Epic Fury, the discussion of prices and the midterms is misplaced. Lower prices and winning elections are good, but a nuclear armed Iran is an existential threat that must be solved regardless of the transient financial impact or election outcome.

Trump usually shares this perspective. For more than 25 years, he has insisted that Iran must not obtain a nuclear weapon. Asked about Vance’s post, Trump acknowledged that the war may have increased gas prices and thereby harmed Republican candidates, but he concluded that “I’d have to do it again because long-term, it’s the only answer. You can’t let Iran have a nuclear weapon.”

Leaders must place survival of their country and its citizens ahead of winning votes. If Trump had been more forthcoming, empathetic, and consistent in his messaging he might have mitigated the sting. Nonetheless, his duty is to America’s continued existence, not his political party’s performance in the midterm elections.

When Trump declared a ceasefire, he dispatched Vance to work out a settlement. The result was a disastrous MOU. As I wrote in RealClearPolitics:

Trump has shown more integrity and grit in the Middle East than any president before him. He restored America’s relationships with Saudi Arabia and the UAE; created a genuine partnership with Israel and expanded it through the Abraham Accords; opened an American era in Syria and Lebanon; and, with Operations Midnight Hammer and Epic Fury, derailed Iran’s nuclear program and severely degraded its military capabilities. He was the best friend Israel – and the Arab states – ever had.

Then, suddenly, his goals shifted. Though he undoubtedly intends America’s friends in the Middle East no harm, Trump abandoned Epic Fury for a “no cost too high” mad dash for a deal. He wanted the MOU in the worst way…. The premature end of Epic Fury shows that foreign-funded and influenced intersectional leftists have hollowed out America’s power, and that Trump lacked the steadfastness needed to overcome the drop in his approval ratings.

Within a week, both parties breached the MOU. I explained:

The MOU was poorly drafted to obtain Iran’s acquiescence. Trump wanted an off ramp, while Iran was a reluctant participant brought along by promises of money, time, and a winnowing of U.S. demands. … Trump and Vice President JD Vance have re-imagined the deal as the one Trump sought instead of the MOU Trump signed; Iran hijacked the first negotiating session to make it about Israel, rather than Iran’s nuclear program; [and] Vance joined the anti-Israel caravan with repeated harsh criticism of its government.

Iran also launched a world-class public relations effort that put to shame Trump’s repeated bluffs of “annihilating” Iran or sending it “back to the stone age.” The far more sophisticated Iranian campaign, aided and abetted by fellow travelers on college campuses and European capitals, portrayed the Revolutionary Guard as freedom fighters and the U.S. as a bully. It painted Iran as a peace-loving nation, even as it continued to execute, starve, and imprison thousands of its citizens, launch indiscriminate attacks on civilians throughout the Middle East, support Houthi attacks on international shipping, and coordinate with Hezbollah and Hamas to attack Israel.

The overwhelming evidence – including admissions made by Iran’s negotiators in meetings with Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner – supports the conclusion that prior to Feb. 28, Iran was, at most, within several months of being able to manufacture up to 11 nuclear warheads, and it was working with Russia, China, and North Korea to perfect ICBMs capable of reaching the United States. Its attack on Diego Garcia shows that its missiles can reach Europe.

Iran has repeatedly called for the destruction of the United States, Israel, Saudi Arabia, U.K., and other countries allied with the United States, and sponsored wide-ranging terrorist attacks on shipping and civilians.

Given its aggression and its amassing and use of an arsenal of more than 7,000 missiles, countless drones, a deep sea navy, and an air force, there is no reason to doubt that if Iran obtained nuclear weapons it would use them against Israel, Saudi Arabia, and the United States. To believe otherwise is to impose Western values on a vengeful Islamic theocracy. Islamic radicals do not fear America’s counterstrike; rather, they seek martyrdom, which the Islamic Circle of North America describes as “the ultimate demonstration of one’s commitment and devotion to God and religious principles.”

If Iran uses nuclear weapons, the price of oil and fertilizer will be the least of our concerns.

news.title: Kai Trump makes very rare comment about mom Vanessa's famous boyfriend
news.text:
Kai Trump has made a very rare comment about her relationship with Tiger Woods, the professional golfer who has been dating her mom, Vanessa, for two years.

The 19-year-old, who is on a golf scholarship at the University of Miami, called him the "best' in a new interview with Golfweek after her appearance at the ANNIKA driven by Gainbridge at Pelican tournament on November 13, 2026.

"I love him so much, and he’s a great guy, and he helps me whenever I want," said Kai, the granddaughter of President Donald Trump, who was pictured still wearing a wrist support, weeks after surgery.

Tiger, 50, is widely regarded as one of the greatest golfers of all time, tied for first in PGA Tour wins, ranked second in men's major championships, and an inductee of the World Golf Hall of Fame.

He began dating Vanessa in late 2024, and they went public in March 2025, when Tiger shared photographs of them on Instagram.

The pair have kept their romance largely private, although Kai included a rare picture of the two together midway through an interview with her mom, posted on Kai's YouTube channel.

In the picture, Vanessa's 17-year-old son Don Jr III towers over his older sister Kai, with Vanessa next to the pair and a beaming Tiger with his arms around Vanessa.

The video was to announce that Vanessa was cancer-free, six months after being diagnosed with breast cancer.

Kai has credited her mom for her love of golf, telling Golfweek: "If it wasn’t for her, I probably wouldn’t be playing golf right now."

Last year, Kai also praised Tiger, calling him "the best golfer in the entire world" and "an even better person."

"He told me to go out there and have fun and just go with the flow. Whatever happens, happens," she said in November 2025.

The ANNIKA driven by Gainbridge at Pelican hosted 108 of the world’s best female professional golfers, including Britain's Charley Hall. Kai was forced to turn down her sponsor invitation after undergoing surgery on her left wrist in early October 2026, the second of the year.

The 19-year-old sustained a wrist injury during her first tournament of the season and decided to undergo surgery for her "long-term health and my future in the game I love."

"It’s certainly not how I envisioned the next few months, but sometimes the journey takes an unexpected turn, and I’m choosing to embrace this one with patience, and a whole lot of determination," the teen captioned a post on Instagram, which featured a picture of Kai in the hospital bed wearing a cast and a black sling.

"Recovery will take time, but I’m incredibly fortunate to be surrounded by amazing people who continue to lift me up, encourage me, and remind me that every challenge is an opportunity to grow," she continued, sharing that family and coaches helped her to make the decision.

"Having the right people by your side makes all the difference, and I couldn’t be more grateful."

news.title: Repair of old copper wiring caused US flight disruption: Trump admin
news.text:
NEW YORK: Weary travelers endured more flight disruptions as service resumed at US airports after an hours-long total stoppage, with officials saying the situation should return to normal Sunday.

The Trump administration blamed the mess that began Friday on a botched replacement of old copper wire communication lines.

The nationwide ground stop — meaning no planes can take off — sparked widespread chaos and left hundreds of thousands of passengers in limbo, with some pulled off planes moments before they were due to depart by airline staff who appeared in the dark about unfolding events.

“Tired. Exhausted. Frustrated. Yeah, you know, it’s just a mess, right?” Lisa Beraid, 48, who works for an insurance company, told AFP as she waited for a flight Saturday morning at New York’s La Guardia airport.

Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) chief Bryan Bedford said that 12,000 flights were canceled on Friday and between four and five thousand flights out of 41,000 scheduled for Saturday were likely to be canceled as well.

But as of Saturday evening, the tracking website FlightAware had recorded more than 6,200 canceled flights.

Speaking at a news conference in Washington, Bedford offered a “sincere apology to the American traveling public.”

He predicted a full resumption of flight schedules by “close of business on Sunday.”

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Friday’s four-hour ground stop was declared after maintenance work to upgrade an old copper wire to a high-speed fiber cable had caused “issues” with communication with airplanes and radar feeds.

“Either through contractor error or a faulty piece of equipment...it started flooding other routers in our air traffic control system,” Duffy told reporters.

In another embarrassment, Saturday’s news conference — where administration officials also appealed for more funds to upgrade outdated systems — was delayed due to technical problems with the audio feed.

Returning to normal

Friday’s disruption was only the second time such a ground stoppage had been issued in US airspace — which is among the busiest in the world — since the 9/11 attacks.

The nationwide halt was lifted at 8:15 p.m. Eastern Time Friday (0115 GMT Saturday).

During the outage, footage from airports showed gates full, with planes waiting on taxiways and passengers thronging concourses, desperate for information.

FAA officials reopened the airspace “after restoring full functionality” at air traffic control facilities, according to Duffy.

Tim Johnson, consumer director at the UK Civil Aviation Authority, said although US flights have resumed, there could be “some follow-on disruption” as airlines re-book passengers and get all services back to normal.

At La Guardia airport, some travelers were more sanguine than others about the continued disruption of their flights.

“We’re stuck here for the next, I don’t know, 36 hours,” said Pat Curlett, a 62-year-old Ford worker.

“No one expects the whole airline system to go down,” said 77-year-old traveler Steven Rathe, who was waiting to embark on a four-leg trip from New York to Albuquerque.

“We’re lucky it wasn’t longer. So they’re flying today and for that I’m grateful.”

Aging infrastructure

The ground stop not only plunged US air travel into chaos — it also raised serious concerns about the country’s aging infrastructure.

Duffy appealed for $50 billion in funds to upgrade and modernize the air traffic control system, and called for Congress, which controls the purse strings of the US government, to “meet this moment.”

“Cut the crap,” retorted Illinois state governor and prominent Democrat, JB Pritzker, on X. “Trump and Republicans have controlled Congress and could have funded the system.”

New York Governor Kathy Hochul called on Duffy to resign or be fired by Trump, writing on X: “We’re fortunate no lives were lost.”

US lawmakers called for investigations into what caused the massive disruption and whether the country is adequately secure from cyber criminality.

“If today proves anything, it’s that we need to update our air traffic control system & rebuild our airport infrastructure,” Republican Senator Eric Schmitt said on X.

President Donald Trump was uncharacteristically quiet about the outage that had knock-on effects for international flights to and from the United States, making no public statement about the ground stop as of Saturday night.

news.title: Trump’s Hannibal Lecter Fixation Takes a Bizarre New Turn
news.text:
President Donald Trump hopped online Saturday evening to rage at his longtime foe Gavin Newsom, while continuing to ignore the mounting travel crisis.

As airports across the country grappled with the fallout from the worst aviation disruption since 9/11, Trump, 80, stayed out of the public eye, posting about his pet projects instead.

In one Truth Social post, the president attacked outgoing California Gov. Gavin Newsom, 57, for commuting the death sentences of all 548 prisoners on death row in the state.

“Some of the people that Gavin Newscum freed from the Death Penalty, after many years of going through the California ‘Justice’ System, make Hannibal Lecter, of Silence of the Lambs, look like a nice guy! President DJT,” Trump wrote. 

The post came nine days after Newsom announced his decision to commute the sentences of California’s death row inmates, and after the California governor had once again taken a series of stabs at Trump and his administration on X. 

While Trump claimed Newsom had “freed” the inmates “from the Death Penalty,” the commutations did not result in anyone being released from prison. Instead, their death sentences were reduced to life without the possibility of parole.

Trump has not made a public appearance since Wednesday. His last on-camera appearance came Thursday, when he sat down for a privately conducted interview with sports commentator Stephen A. Smith at the White House. The president has remained out of sight since the Federal Aviation Administration issued a nationwide ground stop just before 4 p.m. Friday. As of Saturday evening, he had yet to publicly address the aviation crisis.

Trump’s post about Newsom also included his childish nickname for the governor, “Newscum,” just one week after the 80-year-old president told 60 Minutes correspondent Ross Douthat that he could “very easily” resist the urge to name-call Democrats for at least six months in order to work together.

Trump’s decision to invoke fictional serial killer Hannibal Lecter recalled his 2024 presidential campaign, when he spoke so often about the character made famous by Anthony Hopkins that it became the subject of a Saturday Night Live cold open.

On the 2024 campaign trail, Trump repeatedly invoked the “late, great Hannibal Lecter” during rambling speeches about immigration.

“They’re coming from prisons, coming from prisons and jails, you know there is a slight difference... mental institutions, and insane asylums like Silence of the Lamb [sic], the press always says ‘why does he ramble about Silence of the Lamb? Silence of the Lamb, the late, great Hannibal Lecter, he’d like to have you over for dinner. Don’t do it,” Trump said in June 2024 at a campaign stop in Virginia. 

It is unclear whether the president thinks Hannibal Lecter was real. 

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

news.title: Ukraine Says Starshield Restrictions Persist, Hampering Drone Defenses
news.text:
WASHINGTON -- Ukraine says restrictions affecting its use of SpaceX’s Starshield satellite communications system remain widespread, hampering the military’s ability to intercept Russian jet-powered attack drones near the front line and giving Moscow additional opportunities to strike Ukrainian targets.

Denys Sienik, Ukraine’s top diplomat in Washington, told RFE/RL on November 14 that Ukrainian forces continue to experience disruptions despite repeated tests in multiple directions.

“As of today, I can confirm that the restrictions are effective. These are not isolated cases; they are widespread,” Sienik said.

“Because of this, we can intercept Russian jet-powered UAVs only after they enter the territory controlled by Ukraine. Hence, we can’t shoot them down immediately near the front line. This gives Russians more leverage which they haven’t had so far.”

“For example, our Bars units operate using Starshield. They shoot down jet-powered Shaheds. Now we can’t shoot them down there, near the front line,” he said. Instead, Ukrainian forces must wait until the drones reach other defensive lines.

Sienik said the disruptions had persisted for five days, with Ukrainian officials conducting daily tests and obtaining the same results.

SpaceX Denies Restrictions

According to Ukrainian officials who spoke to RFE/RL on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to comment publicly, SpaceX told the ministry: “We are not imposing any restrictions.”

The company referred to technical issues but did not respond to a follow-up question about the situation in temporarily occupied Ukrainian territories, the Ukrainian officials said.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has also challenged SpaceX's explanation, saying Kyiv does not believe the disruptions are simply technical problems.

Zelenskyy said Starshield terminals operating in temporarily Russian-occupied Ukrainian territories had been subject to speed restrictions of approximately 161 kilometers per hour for five days.

He said the restrictions had political implications, arguing that limiting the service in occupied territories risked treating those areas differently from the rest of Ukraine.

“If you impose restrictions there, you are already partially recognizing the temporarily occupied territories as not ours,” Zelenskyy said in remarks released by his office on November 14.

He said he had instructed senior military and foreign ministry officials to pursue the issue with SpaceX and seek the restoration of unrestricted service.

The latest dispute follows a similar episode in October, when Ukrainian officials reported that SpaceX had limited the speed of Starlink and Starshield terminals to approximately 160 kph. Service was reportedly restored on October 24.

SpaceX founder Elon Musk has maintained that Starshield is controlled by the US government, with the military determining restrictions on speed and use and the final authority resting with President Donald Trump. Trump has denied involvement in the restrictions.

Democrats Seek Answers

The disruptions have also drawn growing concern in Washington, where lawmakers from both parties have questioned the extent of private control over communications systems used in Ukraine's defense.

Democratic Senators Jeanne Shaheen and Chris Coons, both members of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, have formally asked Musk to preserve all records related to restrictions on Ukraine's use of Starlink and Starshield.

In a letter made public on November 13, the senators requested documents and communications dating back to September 1, including exchanges involving Musk, SpaceX executives, Ukrainian officials, the White House, and the Pentagon.

They also asked Musk to confirm by November 30 that appropriate safeguards were in place.

Democratic lawmakers in the House also condemned reports of renewed limitations.

Gregory Meeks, the ranking Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, and Adam Smith, the ranking Democrat on the House Armed Services Committee, said any restrictions on Ukraine's use of Starshield in occupied territories and along the line of contact would be unacceptable if confirmed.

They argued that previous limitations had contributed to Ukrainian civilian casualties, including the deaths of children, and strengthened Russia's position.

The lawmakers pledged to continue pressing for answers and accountability.

Experts Warn Of Dependence

The dispute has renewed questions about Ukraine's dependence on a single private company for critical military communications.

Retired US Army Lieutenant Colonel Amos Fox, a fellow at Arizona State University's Future Security Initiative, told RFE/RL that the situation illustrates the risks of relying on a single provider for essential military capabilities.

“A challenger to Musk’s dominance of this space would help insulate states like Ukraine from the political games of people like Musk,” Fox said.

He also pointed to the influence that individuals outside government can exercise over national security decisions when states depend heavily on their companies and resources.

Paul Poast of the University of Chicago questioned whether the disruptions could be explained by technical problems alone.

While acknowledging that technology outages can occur, Poast told RFE/RL that he doubted the Starshield disruption was simply a glitch.

He noted Musk's previous comments that an earlier slowdown resulted from SpaceX's interpretation of its terms of service and questioned whether the latest disruptions could be connected to diplomatic efforts involving Ukraine and Russia.

Poast raised the possibility that the disruptions could have served as an indirect means of increasing pressure on Kyiv during negotiations, although he offered no evidence establishing such a connection.

Dispute Amid Talks

The Starshield dispute comes as the Trump administration seeks to advance negotiations to end Russia's full-scale war against Ukraine, with questions over territorial concessions and European security remaining contentious.

US special envoy Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner -- Trump's son-in-law -- said they remained in contact with Moscow, Kyiv, and European partners following trilateral discussions.

In a social media statement on November 14, Kushner said the next phase of negotiations would focus on facilitating direct engagement between Russia and European governments and preparing another round of trilateral talks.

He said several new ideas were being explored and stressed that any eventual agreement must include credible security guarantees for Ukraine.

“President Trump will only support arrangements that strengthen Ukraine’s and Europe’s security and make future conflict less likely,” Kushner wrote.

His comments followed criticism from Republican Senator Tom Cotton, who rejected reported Russian demands that NATO withdraw forces from Eastern Europe.

“NATO nations withdrawing from their own borders is a preposterous demand by Russia,” Cotton said, adding that Moscow would stop fighting only when it understood it could not win.

European leaders have also warned against pressuring Kyiv into territorial concessions.

French President Emmanuel Macron said on November 14 that countries seeking to limit assistance to Ukraine were effectively trying to impose an unjust peace, warning that such an approach could lead to another war.

The White House and Pentagon had not responded to requests for comment on the latest Starshield disruptions as of late November 14.

news.title: US threatening to starve Iranians – Tehran
news.text:
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei has accused the US of threatening to starve his country’s population through sanctions and a naval blockade.

Speaking after a G7 foreign ministers’ meeting in Paris on Tuesday, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio described the “economic pain” inflicted on Tehran as “extraordinary,” warning that the impact of the restrictions would intensify over time.

He argued that mounting hardship could force Tehran’s leadership to make concessions, as “eventually you have to eat.”

“This is yet another admission that Washington is pursuing war crimes, compounding the atrocities it has already committed in its wars of aggression and economic terrorism against Iran,” Baghaei wrote on X on Saturday.

“After decades of failed coercion, threats, sanctions, terrorism, and aggression, the United States continues to repeat the same mistakes, merely repackaging them under new names,” he added.

The US began blockading Iran’s southern ports in April after Tehran closed the Strait of Hormuz, a vital oil and LNG shipping route, in response to the US-Israeli bombing campaign launched on February 28.

In August, the US launched Operation Economic Outcast, with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent threatening the “economic asphyxiation” of Iran through sweeping sanctions targeting Iranian businesses and their foreign partners.

Iran has also accused the US of striking civilian water infrastructure, including desalination facilities and drinking-water reservoirs, disrupting supplies to thousands of residents. Washington denied responsibility for a March attack on a desalination plant on Qeshm Island and said its June strikes targeted military communications and radar facilities.

Tensions remain high despite President Donald Trump saying that new large-scale strikes were unlikely. The US has reportedly warned Israel and Gulf states to prepare for a possible resumption of combat operations.

Washington previously rejected Iran’s terms for reopening the Strait of Hormuz, which included lifting US sanctions, releasing frozen Iranian assets, and ending hostilities on “all fronts,” including Israel’s wars in Gaza and southern Lebanon.

“The ball is now in the American court,” Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, Tehran’s chief negotiator, said on Wednesday.

Rubio dismissed Iran’s conditions as “absurd,” while Trump said on Thursday that Washington no longer needed a deal with Tehran because “those days have long since passed.”

news.title: Nigeria and Walls of Jericho: A review of Lasisi Olagungu’s ‘Masks and Tears’
news.text:
Many things have been written about Nigeria and issues in Nigeria. Still, author and award-winning journalist, Lasisi Olagungu, in one of his new books that will be unveiled at the University of Ibadan on Tuesday, 24 November, 2026, titled ‘Masks and Tears: Reflections on Nigeria and Its Times’, tells us that the country is where it is today, with its many troubles, because “Dysfunctional Nigeria is built of stuffs stronger than the Walls of Jericho.” Therefore, the noise and the wailing of ordinary Nigerians at the nadir, where chaos and emergencies are common, cannot reach the ears of the principalities and powers who lead and rule the country from the impassable high walls.

‘Masks and Tears’ is a 627-page compendium of the author’s Monday Lines column published every Monday in the Nigerian Tribune newspaper. The book, published recently by Safari Books, contains 84 thought-provocative essays that span from Monday, May 4, 2020 to Monday, October 23, 2022.

Keen spectators of the Nigerian Project and its managers know that this was the period Nigeria and Nigerians had to contend with the coronavirus pandemic, the EndSARS protests, school and industrial strikes, farmer-herder conflicts, the late President Muhammadu Buhari’s slow-motion government, the aggressive politicking ahead of the 2023 elections, and the many political, social, economic, and religious upheavals that shaped the collective existential milieu of Nigeria.

‘Masks and Tears’, as its subtitle ‘Reflections on Nigeria and Its Times’ suggests, serves as a history book that chronicles those consequential local and national events through Olagungu’s constant eagle-eye view on national and international issues, journalistic stewardship, and meticulous penmanship.

A conscious read of the book from the first essay, ‘Death and Dying Emirs’, to the last one, ‘Peter Obi and His Enemies’, reveals that the author, with his acerbic pen, spares no one and nothing he focuses his interest on. He says it the way it is — in plain, simple English — in a manner a primary school pupil can understand.

There are many big names and personalities mentioned in the book, many of whom most people would shudder when they speak or catch a cold when they sneeze. Donald Trump, Muhammadu Buhari, Olusegun Obasanjo, Bola Tinubu, Atiku Abubakar, Peter Obi, Nasir El-Rufai, Adams Oshiomole, Ibrahim Gambari, Mamman Daura, Abiola Ajimobi, Hakeem Baba-Ahmed, Bisi Akande, Chris Ngige, and a long list of others. They are all in there.

READ ALSO: Lasisi Olagunju: The Gong of the Masses

However, Olugungu, as he tells us in the dedication of the book, comes from a lineage whose “fathers never answered the king gently” and whose “Children answered kings with defiance.” So, in all the 84 essays in the book, the author literally looks big men and women in the eye and tells them the hard truth. And, interestingly, he tells his truth without name-calling, but with the craftiness of the unusual rat who bites you gently and at the same time blows you a soft breeze so that you would not know it is biting you. He does this skillfully with proverbs and metaphors, and sometimes in his native Yoruba language that, most of the time, he deliberately refuses to translate into English.

‘Masks and Tears’ is an unusual book, but so is its main character, Nigeria, and its many troubles. Since 1897 that Flora Shaw — wife of British colonial administrator Sir Frederick Lugard — coined the name Nigeria, to the 1914 amalgamation of the country, to the 1960 independence, to the current times, Nigeria has defied many cures to its troubles. In ‘Masks and Tears’, it is easy to see that Nigeria shares many dispositions with an intractable woman, a bad wife. Any attempt to write a book on how to make such a woman behave will wear the writer out. But Olugunju is no ordinary writer. From his interventions in the book, it is evident that he has mastered the patience, art, and language of managing the many eccentricities of Nigeria when most Nigerians have divorced or are seeking to divorce her.

However, the author knows that divorce is not the answer to the marital quandaries with Nigeria. He knows that divorce will only harden and heighten the Walls of Jericho that entrap the country. He notes this in the essay ‘Nigerians’ Anger and the Coming Darkness’, where he writes, “The country keeps doing horror to the people without consequences.” Then, he asks, “So, how do we pull back from this precipice of chaos?” But the bard does not politick, legislate, or even advise. He only beams light on the good and evil that man and his society create for themselves.

From the title of the book and also from the titles of the essays that make it up, one might perceive that the author is cut out for doom commentary. But the writer only writes about what society feeds to his consciousness, and Nigeria has so many troubles to abuse the consciousness and creative spirit of an observer. The least the author has done with the book, through subtle defiance and creative protest, is to offer history and, perhaps, a warning.

There is a seminal book on the origins of power, prosperity, and poverty, titled ‘Why Nations Fail’ by Daron Acemoglu and James Robinson. The book can help you understand why Nigeria is failing and falling. Suffering and smiling, like Fela Anikulapo Kuti sings. Obafemi Awolowo’s ‘The People’s Republic’, Chinua Achebe’s ‘The Trouble with Nigeria’, Niyi Osundare’s ‘Dialogue With My Country’, Lasisi Olagunju’s ‘Cowries of Blood’, and other similar books can give you further insight into the troubles with Nigeria. But the unique thing about Olugungu’s ‘Masks and Tears’ is that it shines more light on the most recent troubles of the country as they unfold every week, every Monday, leveraging deep wisdom from Yoruba proverbs and his vast knowledge of over three decades of journalism practice.

From the very first page of the book to the last one, the language deployed in writing the essays is easy to read and understand. The style the author adopts is easy to recognise across the 84 essays to the point that if you read any of them without his name on it, you can rightly guess it is the author who wrote it. The voice is simple but clear, as if the author is telling you about the events every week as they unfold in the manner a father tells his child nighttime stories.

Equally of note is the physical quality of the book. The book is printed on durable paper, and the cover design properly reflects the import and seriousness of its title.

‘Masks and Tears’ is a book that addresses big national problems. It is a consequential book that brooks no pretence to the stark realities of Nigeria and Nigerians. news.title: Kai Trump opens up about her close bond with mom Vanessa’s boyfriend Tiger Woods
news.text:
Kai Trump has opened up about her close relationship with golf legend Tiger Woods, praising her mom Vanessa Trump’s boyfriend for constantly offering pointers and support on and off the course.

Speaking to Golfweek following her appearance at The ANNIKA driven by Gainbridge at Pelican tournament on November 13, the 19-year-old University of Miami golfer and granddaughter of President Donald Trump shared how frequently she turns to the 50-year-old icon for advice.

“He’s the best,” Kai said of Woods, who went public with his relationship with Vanessa—the ex-wife of Donald Trump Jr.—in March 2025. “I love him so much, and he’s a great guy, and he helps me whenever I want.”

Kai also credited her mother for putting a club in her hand when she was just two years old, noting: “If it wasn’t for her, I probably wouldn’t be playing golf right now.”

She added that she also regularly tees off with her 80-year-old grandfather.

‘Go Out There and Have Fun’

It isn't the first time the rising collegiate golfer has highlighted Woods' mentorship. Following her ANNIKA debut back in November 2025, Kai praised both his athletic legacy and his calm advice ahead of high-pressure tournaments.

“I mean, he is the best golfer in the entire world, I would say that. And an even better person,” she told reporters at the time. “He told me to go out there and have fun and just go with the flow. Whatever happens, happens.”

Standing Together Through Tough Personal Battles

Behind the scenes, Woods—who shares daughter Sam, 19, and son Charlie, 17, with ex-wife Elin Nordegren—has reportedly become a steady pillar for Vanessa and her five children with Don Jr. (Kai, Donald, 17, Tristan, 15, Spencer, 14, and Chloe, 12), particularly after Vanessa revealed her breast cancer diagnosis in May.

“I am staying focused and hopeful while surrounded by the love and support of my family, my kids and those closest to me,” Vanessa wrote on Instagram when sharing the news.

A source close to the family previously told PEOPLE that Woods "has been there for [Vanessa] as much as she wants it," adding that supporting her allowed him to "forget his own problems for a while and show his love and support for a real trooper of a girlfriend."

That support has been mutual. news.title: Vance Is Right: The Iran War Lost Republicans the Midterms
news.text:
The morning after Republicans suffered the most devastating midterm loss in recent memory, Vice President JD Vance posted his response to the election results on X. Vance’s poignant diagnosis has garnered over 72 million views and widespread support from both the administration and voters on the right.

To riff off a famous line from President Bill Clinton’s strategist James Carville, Vance’s midterm manifesto basically boiled down to one thing: “It’s the war, stupid.”

And Vance is right. The Iran war was overwhelmingly unpopular, especially amongst young voters.

Predictably, pundits like Marc Thiessen and The Wall Street Journal editorial board were quick to blame the loss on anything but the war. Instead of owning up to their miscalculations, they doubled down on their stale warmongering and went straight for President Donald Trump’s most popular (and successful) policies: tariffs and immigration.

In their efforts to label Vance’s diagnosis as a break from the president, war-loving neoconservatives like Thiessen themselves utterly betrayed Trump and the American people.

Americans care about affordability, simple as that. Trump’s tariffs and immigration crackdown opened up jobs right here at home and were largely popular with the American people.

The Iran war was not.

news.title: History Says This Is the Best Investing Move You Can Make if a Bear Market Is Coming
news.text:
Right now, the U.S. stock market feels a little shaky. Inflation is still well above target. The Federal Reserve is on track to raise interest rates again next month. And the Iran war shows no signs of ending.

The S&P 500 (^GSPC -0.40%) is down a modest 3% in the last month, while the Nasdaq-100 is off nearly 10%.

All of this is to say that many investors are considering the possibility of a bear market right now. While earnings expectations for U.S. companies are still looking strong, there are enough concerns about the future of the artificial intelligence (AI) building boom, the biggest driver of recent economic growth, that investors are looking at ways to protect themselves.

And it's a good thing, too. The best time to think about your investment process is before something happens.

The dip you're waiting for probably isn't the bottom

Market declines tend to trigger some of the worst investor behaviors. If stocks are declining, there's an inclination to stay away because 10% drawdowns often become 20% to 30%. It happened in 2000-2002, 2007-2009, and 2022.

But those declines also have a recent history of rebounding quickly, often before investors even noticed. These occurred in late 2018 and early 2025 during President Donald Trump's Liberation Day tariffs, and in the more extreme case of the COVID pandemic.

In other words, nobody knows whether a correction is the end or the beginning of a deeper drawdown. And even if you did know which one it was going to be, market timing requires you to be right twice: once when you decide to get out of the market and once when you later get back in. Plus, that requires a discipline many investors lack.

Automating your investing is the better process

You can still take advantage of lower share prices during bear markets by simply maintaining your monthly investing schedule. If you have money going into a brokerage account every month or every paycheck into something like a 401(k), keep doing what you're doing.

This process allows you to buy the dips and lower your average cost without worrying about whether it's the right time to trade. Plus, bear markets often last far less time than the average bull market.

If you try to time the market, there's a good chance that the rebound will have already started once you decide it's OK to return to stocks. By automating, you may not get the absolute lowest prices on your purchases, but you'll certainly get at least some at discounted prices.

As always, investing is one of the few things where doing less can yield better results.
news.summary: Should investors wait for stocks to fall before buying?

news.title: Global powers converge on Manila as ASEAN summit kicks off
news.text:
MANILA – A key regional summit opens on Nov 15 in Manila, with South-east Asian heads of state facing questions on trade, security and an ongoing energy crisis while playing host to a “who’s who” of global leaders.

US President Donald Trump is scheduled to arrive on Nov 17 near the summit’s conclusion, a visit expected to include a sideline meeting with fellow Quad countries India, Japan and Australia – the first of his second term.

The meeting of the Quad – a grouping broadly aimed at counterbalancing China’s regional influence – would come days before a historic sit-down with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russia’s Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen.

Brazil’s recently re-elected Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, meanwhile, is set to attend a plenary session of the 11-member Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) on Nov 15, while Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese will sign a new defence pact with host country the Philippines.

Nearly 20,000 police officers have been deployed around Metro Manila for the summit, with progressive groups predicting a turnout of thousands on Nov 17 for an anti-Trump march on the summit site.

Much of the uproar targets the US Pax Silica programme – a supply-chain initiative designed to counter China’s dominance in semiconductors and rare earths – whose flagship Philippine project, a 1,620ha AI manufacturing hub north of Manila, threatens to displace Indigenous families.

US Ambassador to the Philippines Lee Lipton said last week that a widely rumoured November target date for a deal signing timed to Trump’s visit was never in the works.

Unfinished business

A day of early meetings kicked off on Nov 14 with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney announcing a Philippine trade deal, and ASEAN leaders huddling on key issues including haze from Indonesia and potential fuel-sharing schemes as members struggle with Iran war-driven shortages.

But two issues that have vexed ASEAN leaders for years – a languishing South China Sea “Code of Conduct” and their relationship with war-torn Myanmar – look to be Singapore’s problem when the bloc’s rotating chair passes to the city-state in 2027.

Myanmar has been excluded from high-level ASEAN meetings since a 2021 military coup that ousted the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi and triggered an ongoing civil war.

Thailand, which shares a border with Myanmar and is leading the charge for closer relations, last week called for Naypyidaw’s foreign minister to be allowed back into meetings.

But Philippine foreign secretary Theresa Lazaro told reporters on Nov 14 there was “no easing” of the approach being taken with Myanmar, which faces an international ruling later this week on whether it committed genocide against its marginalised Muslim Rohingya minority.

Hopes of achieving a so-called Code of Conduct in the disputed South China Sea between ASEAN states and China during Manila’s year in the chair, meanwhile, have flagged.

A South-east Asian diplomat involved in summit preparations told AFP he did not expect a code to be signed at the summit.

Lazaro indicated as much on Nov 14, saying negotiations were “80%” complete.

“If it happens, then it’s a small miracle,” said Siew Mun Tang, former head of the ASEAN Studies Centre at Singapore’s ISEAS-Yusof Ishak Institute.

Shadow of Beijing

Beijing claims most of the South China Sea despite an international ruling that its assertion has no legal basis, and its coast guard has clashed repeatedly with that of the Philippines.

The row has reared its head at inopportune times over the past year, with a July foreign ministers summit opening less than a day after Chinese and Philippine sailors engaged in a clash.

An ASEAN defence chiefs meeting in October saw Beijing send only an embassy defence attache, blaming “reckless” statements by Philippine politicians.

A week later, Manila issued a rare rebuke to its own public officials over comments about China, stressing the need for a unified voice as the two countries negotiate.

As the summit opens on Nov 15, an annual seminar less than 5km away will be making the case against China’s South China Sea claims.

Philippine defence chief Gilberto Teodoro, sanctioned by Beijing in 2026 for what it called “irresponsible remarks”, will give a keynote address. AFP
